<>Can2d2a1las and allowed the brahmin to go free.
<NI>Escaping from there Bharata reached a village walking
<>all the way. That village was being ruled over by a
<>king called Rahu1gan2a and that king was going to see
<>Bhagava1n Kapila Mahars2i along the banks of the river
<>Iks2umati1 in a palanquin. The palanquin had not enough [Page120-b+ 63]
<>bearers and so the brahmin was asked to join the

<NI>Bharata went from there to the forests singing devo-
<>tional songs in praise of Vis2n2u and at last attained

<HI>BHARATA IV. A sage and the famous author of Na1t2ya-
<>s4a1stra. He was a critic who lived around the year 400

<>famous. Ka1lida1sa in the second act of his drama,
<>Vikramorvas4i1ya states that this Bharata used to coach

<>comprising thirtyseven chapters dealing with the art of

<>been written by lions in the profession: Mitragupta,
<>Hars2avardhana, S4an3kuka, Udbhat2a, Bhat2t2ana1yaka and
<>Abhinavagupta. Of these ‘Abhinavabha1rati1’ the com-
<>mentary written by Abhinavagupta is the only one
<>freely available now.
<HI>BHARATA V. The Maha1bha1rata speaks about a few

<HI>BHA1RATA (MAHA1BHA1RATA). An epic written by
<>Vya1sa.
<NI>1) {%General information.%} The Maha1bha1rata is an epic.
<>Bharata is acclaimed as the first emperor of Bha1rata.
<>The theme of this great epic is the fight between the

<>The great size of the volume and the greatness of

<>to its getting the name, Maha1bha1rata. Once the
<>devas put the Maha1bha1rata in one pan of a balance
<>and the Vedas in the other pan. Then the devas

<>than all the Vedas put together. (S4lokas 269-271,
<>Chapter 1, A1di Parva, M.B.).

<NI>(1) {%A1di Parva.%} (A1di = beginning). Pa1n2d2u and Dhr2ta-

<NI>(2) {%Sabha1 Parva%} (Sabha1 = court). The Pa1n2d2avas and

<NI>(5) {%Bhi1s2ma Parva%} (Bhi1s2ma = The first Generalissimo of

<NI>(6) {%Dron2a Parva%} (Dron2a = The second Generalissimo).

<NI>3) {%Mode of Narration.%} Most of the verses in the

<>matter is purely mundane.

<NI>This fixing of the date of Maha1bha1rata is based on the
<>conclusions arrived at by the pandits of Bha1rata, but
<>foreign chronologists differ from us. They argue that
<>it was in the 10th century B.C. that the Maha1bha1rata
<>battle took place on the strength of the following:
<NI>The theme of the Maha1bha1rata is a fight between
<>Kurus and Pa1n5ca1las. After the war the two join and
<>there is a statement in the Yajurveda of a people
<>formed by the merger of the two. Therefore the great
<>war should have happened in the 10th century B.C. It
<>was a period of hero-worship and songs on the heroic
<>deeds of the Kurus and Pa1n2d2avas were sung and
<>handed over from one generation to the other and
<>gradually those songs took shape in the form of the
<>Maha1bha1rata.
<NI>There is another school of thought. In the Maha1-
<>bha1rata, Brahma1 is given great prominence. But in
<>Vedic times Brahma1 was not counted at all. During
<>the golden period of the Buddhists Brahma1 had a cons-
<>picuous hold on Hinduism. Therefore it should be
<>deduced that the Maha1bha1rata was written during the
<>6th century B.C. Then there were about 8,000 verses
<>in the Maha1bha1rata.
<NI>Towards the second stage of Maha1bha1rata the epic
<>grew in size bringing into its fold about 24,000 s4lokas.
<>It was at this stage that the Maha1bha1rata got a vais2n2a-
<>vite colour and S4ri1 Kr2s2n2a was adored as an incarnation
<>of Vis2n2u. Megasthenes who visited India in 300 B.C.
<>records that the majority of Hindus were vais2n2avites
<>at that period. There are references in certain parts [Page123-b+ 61]
<>of the Maha1bha1rata to Greeks and Buddhists. There-

<HI>BHA1SA. A very prominent dramatist in Sanskrit. As
<>Ba1n2a and Ka1lida1sa have noticed him in their works,
<>it may safely be assumed that Bha1sa lived in an earlier
<>period. Since Pratima1 na1t2aka and Abhis2eka na1t2aka,
<>which are universally admitted to have been composed
<>by Bha1sa, depend for their themes on the Va1lmi1ki [Page126-b+ 65]
<>Ra1ma1yan2a, it is clear that Bha1sa lived after Va1lmi1ki.
<>Ka1lida1sa's period has not yet been fixed beyond doubt.
<>It is almost settled that Ba1n2a lived sometime between the
<>sixth and seventh centuries A.D. Prof. Keith has been
<>of the view that Va1lmi1ki lived before the 4th century
<>B.C. In the light of all such factors it could be presumed
<>that Bha1sa lived in the period between the 4th century
<>B.C. and 6th century A.D.
<NI>Though Bha1sa has so many glories to his credit he does
<>not fully match Ka1lida1sa, and this might have been the
<>reason why Indians did almost forget Bha1sa with the
<>advent of Ka1lida1sa on the literary arena.
<NI>We are not in a position to name with unerring definite-
<>ness the works of Bha1sa. The general belief is that he
<>has written nearly twenty three dramas. In 1922, Pandit
<>Gan2apati S4a1stri1 unearthed from various sources thirteen
<>dramas of Bha1sa. Three out of them, viz. Pratijn5a1-
<>yaugandhara1yan2a, S4vapnava1savadatta and Avima1-
<>raka owe their themes to the Br2hatkatha1, while Prati-
<>ma1 na1t2aka and Abhis2eka na1t2aka have Ra1ma1yan2a as
<>their basic inspiration. Out of the eight remaining
<>dramas six, viz. Madhyama vya1yoga, Pan5cara1tra, Du1ta-
<>va1kya, Du1taghat2otkaca, Karn2abha1ra and U1rubhan3ga
<>owe their themes to the Maha1bha1rata, while the last
<>two dramas, Ba1lacarita and Ca1rudatta are dependent
<>for their themes on anecdotes about S4ri1 Kr2s2n2a and on
<>yaks2a stories.
<NI>Though Dr. Gan2apati S4a1stri1 has strongly contended that
<>all the above thirteen dramas were written by Bha1sa
<>himself, his view has not yet received universal accep-
<>tance. Whatever that be, it is an admitted fact that
<>Svapnava1savadatta is by far the best among the thirteen
<>dramas. It is a continuation of the story of Pratijn5a1yau-
<>gandhara1yan2a. The wedding of king Udayana and
<>Va1savadatta1 is the subject matter of Svapnava1sava-
<>datta.
<NI>With his killing of the Ra1ks2asa ‘Avi’ the Sauvi1ra king
<>comes to be known as Avima1ra, and Avima1ra's falling
<>in love with Kuran3gi1, daughter of Kuntibhoja forms the
<>theme of the drama, Avima1raka. In Pratima1 na1t2aka
<>is told the story narrated in Ra1ma1yan2a from Ayodhya1-
<>ka1n2d2a to Pat2t2a1bhis2eka. Abhis2eka na1t2aka codifies the
<>stories in the Kis2kindha1 Ka1n2d2a and Sundara Ka1n2d2a of
<>the R2a1ma1yan2a and describes the coronations of Sugri1va
<>and of S4ri1 Ra1ma. Though the characters in Pan5cara1tra
<>are borrowed from Maha1bha1rata the story is entirely
<>Bha1sa's. Madhyama vya1yoga, Du1tava1kya, Du1taghat2ot-
<>kaca, Karn2abha1ra and U1rubhan3ga are one-act plays.
<>These five plays have as their basis some of the anecdotes
<>in the Maha1bha1rata. In Ca1rudatta is treated the love
<>story of Ca1rudatta and Vasantasena1.
<NI>Indisputable evidence is still lacking to credit Bha1sa
<>with the authorship of all the thirteen plays referred to
<>above.

<HI>BHAVABHU1TI. A Sanskrit poet who lived in the 7th
<>century A.D. His important works are the three dramas,
<>Ma1lati1ma1dhava, Maha1vi1racarita and Uttarara1ma-
<>carita. Bhavabhu1ti was a brahmin of the Kas4yapa-
<>gotra. He was the son of one Ni1lakan2t2ha and one Ja1tu-
<>karn2i1. He was a great devotee of S4iva and he got his
<>name Bhavabhu1ti later because of this. His original
<>name was Ni1lakan2t2ha. Bhavabhu1ti was born in Padma-
<>pura in the state of Vidarbha. But Bhavabhu1ti spent
<>most of his life in the palace of Yas4odharma1, king of
<>Kannauj.
<NI>Bhavabhu1ti's first drama is believed to be Maha1vi1ra-
<>carita. There are seven acts in this. The theme is based
<>on the story of S4ri1 Ra1ma. But there are some variations
<>from the original Ra1ma1yan2a in this drama. Bhava-
<>bhu1ti states that even at the time of the svayam3vara of
<>Si1ta1, Ra1van2a was a suitor. There is an opinion among
<>certain critics that Bhavabhu1ti did write only up to the
<>46th verse in the fourth act and the rest was written
<>by another poet named Subrahman2ya.
<NI>Ma1lati1ma1dhava is a drama of ten acts. It is a love-story
<>of Ma1lati1 and Ma1dhava. Ma1lati1 was the daughter of the
<>minister of Ujjayini1 and Madhava was the son of the
<>minister of Vidarbha. It was while Ma1dhava was having
<>his education in Ujjayini1 that he came to love Ma1lati1.
<>It was Ka1mandaki1 who was a classmate of both the
<>ministers and who became a sannya1sini1 later who pulls
<>the strings of this love story. The king of Ujjayini1 wanted
<>Ma1lati1 to marry Nandana, a friend of his. But Ma1lati1
<>did not love him. Yet afraid of getting the displeasure of
<>the King, Ma1lati1's father decided to give her in marriage
<>to Nandana. In despair Ma1dhava was about to commit
<>suicide when from the temple nearby Ma1dhava heard
<>an agonised weeping. He rushed to the site of the sound
<>and found to his bewilderment the gruesome sight of
<>Ma1lati1 being dragged for sacrifice by a sorceress named
<>Kapa1lakun2d2ala1 helped by her guru Aghoraghan2t2a.
<>Ma1dhava killed Aghoraghan2t2a and saved Ma1lati1.
<>Disappointed Kapa1lakun2d2ala1 swore that she would
<>seek revenge on Ma1dhava and disappeared. Ma1lati1
<>went back to her palace. At this time Madayantika1,
<>sister of Nandana and Makaranda, a friend of Ma1dhava
<>became lovers. Once Madayantika1 was attacked by a
<>tiger in a S4iva temple and Makaranda saved her from [Page128-a+ 63]
<>the wild beast, and they became lovers thereafter. The
<>proposal to give Ma1lati1 in marriage to Nandana was
<>still pending then. The marriage day was fixed and a
<>day before that by a clever ruse played by the keen-
<>witted Ka1mandaki1 Ma1lati1 and Ma1dhava eloped together.
<>Makaranda, friend of Ma1dhava, was disguised and dressed
<>in bridal robes and Nandana little suspecting the trick
<>played on him married the substitute. Before they went
<>to the bridal chamber for the night Nandana's sister
<>came to see her new sister-in-law and the moment she
<>put her eyes on her she understood who it was and that
<>night they also eloped. Thus poor Nandana was left
<>alone.
<NI>Kapa1lakun2d2ala1 by her sorcery separated Ma1lati1 from
<>Ma1dhava but luckily Sauda1mini1 a disciple of Ka1man-
<>taki1 saved her from Kapa1lakun2d2ala1. Later Ma1lati1
<>married Ma1dhava with the permission of the King.
<>This is the story of Ma1lati1-Ma1dhava.
<NI>Uttarara1macarita is a play of seven acts. The theme is
<>the story of Ra1ma after his return to Ayodhya1 after the
<>exile. It begins with the renouncement of Si1ta1 by Ra1ma

<NI>All these three dramas used to be enacted during the
<>festival of ‘Ka1lapriyana1tha’ at Ujjayini1. The predomi-
<>nant emotion in Maha1vi1racarita is ‘Vi1ra’, in Ma1lati1-
<>Ma1dhava, ‘Sr2n3ga1ra’ and in Uttarara1macarita ‘Karun2a’.
<>In expressing and elaborating the emotion of ‘Karun2a’
<>Bhavabhu1ti excels Ka1lida1sa. The one draw-back which
<>keeps him second to Ka1lida1sa is his lack of humour and
<>wit. The sanskrit poet Dhanapa1la in his book’
<>‘Tilakaman5jari’ speaks about Bhavabhu1ti thus:
<Poem>Spas2t2abha1varasa1 citraih2

<HI>BHI1MA. Bhi1masena, one of the five Pa1n2d2avas.
<F>1) Since much information about Bhi1ma is given under the captions Dharmaputra, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva and Pa1n5ca1li1 only
<>a brief description of Bhi1ma is attempted under the present heading.</F>
<NI>1) {%Genealogy.%} (See genealogy of Arjuna).
<NI>2) {%Birth and childhood.%} King Vicitravi1rya of Candra
<>vam3s4a (lunar dynasty) had two sons called Dhr2ta-
<>ra1s2t2ra and Pa1n2d2u. The Kauravas (Duryodhana etc.) were
<>sons born to Dhr2tara1s2t2ra of his wife Ga1ndha1ri1, and the [Page129-a+ 65]
<>Pa1n2d2avas were the sons of Pa1n2d2u and his wives Kunti1
<>and Ma1dri1. Dharmaputra, Bhi1ma and Arjuna were
<>the sons of Kunti1, and Nakula and Sahadeva of
<>Ma1dri1.
<F>1) The Pa1n2d2avas were not in fact direct issues of Pa1n2d2u. For details see Kunti1.</F>
<NI>Kunti1 directed a mantra gifted to her by Durva1sas to-
<>wards Va1yubhagava1n (the wind-god) and the result
<>was the birth of Bhi1ma. Hence he is called Va1yu-putra
<>(son of the wind-god). At the time of his birth a celestial
<>voice announced that the boy would grow up to be the
<>strongest among the strong. (A1di Parva, Chapter 122,
<>Verse 14). On the tenth day after birth the child Bhi1ma
<>fell from his mother's lap on a rock. Bhi1ma was not
<>injured in any manner by that fall, although it crushed
<>the rock into power. (This story is told in the southern
<>texts of the Maha1bha1rata in Chapter 132 of A1di Parva).
<>The naming ceremony of the child was performed by
<>the Mahars2is, who stayed at S4atas4r2n3ga. Kas4yapa Maha-
<>rs2i, family priest of Vasudeva performed the ceremonies
<>like wearing of the sacred thread. Bhi1ma learned fight-
<>ing with the gada1 (club or mace) from S4uka, the famous
<>Ra1jars2i.
<NI>The Kauravas and the Pa1n2d2avas spent their childhood
<>in Hastina1pura. Dron2a1ca1rya taught them fighting
<>with weapons. The Kauravas and the Pa1n2d2avas often
<>engaged themselves in children's games. In all such
<>games Bhi1ma used to hurt and defeat the Kauravas,
<>and to this fact the unending hatred of the Kauravas
<>towards Bhi1ma owed its origin. Once they adminis-
<>tered poison to Bhi1ma who fell down unconscious, and
<>then they threw him into the depths of the Gan3ga1
<>(Ganges). Going deeper and deeper in the waters
<>Bhi1ma, at last, reached the Na1galoka, where the na1gas
<>(serpents) bit him which neutralized the effects of the
<>poison in his body. There he got acquainted with a
<>na1ga called A1ryaka, who introduced him to Va1suki,
<>king of the na1gas, and Va1suki presented him with much
<>wealth and other costly gems. But, what use was all
<>this wealth to Bhi1ma? Then Va1suki agreed to give him
<>a divine drink, which would give the user of it the
<>strength of thousand elephants. Bhi1ma drank at one
<>draught eight pot-fulls of that divine drink, and thus
<>became tremendously strong. But, he had to wait in
<>Na1galoka for eight days so that the drink might be
<>thoroughly assimilated, and on the ninth day the na1gas
<>saw him off in all pomp and splendour. Bhi1ma returned
<>to his mother and brothers and consoled them, who
<>were terribly anxious at his absence.
<NI>When the training of the princes in the use of weapons
<>was over a competition or test was conducted. Duryo-
<>dhana and Bhi1ma entered into a ‘club-fight’, and when
<>Karn2a tried to intervene in the fight his nobility was
<>questioned by Bhi1ma. Duryodhana then insulted Bhi1ma.
<>Arjuna agreed to present King Drupada before Dron2a1-
<>ca1rya as gurudaks2ina1 to him. In the fierce war the
<>Pa1n2d2avas fought with Drupada, Bhi1ma annihilated the
<>elephant division of the latter's army. And, afterwards
<>Bhi1ma underwent higher training in club-war at the
<>hands of Balabhadrara1ma. (A1di Parva, Chapter 136,
<>Verse 4).
<NI>3) {%The Pa1n2d2avas left Hastina1pura.%} As enmity between
<>the Kauravas and the Pa1n2d2avas began growing stronger
<>and stronger, Duryodhana, with his father's permission,
<>removed the Pa1n2d2avas to va1ran2a1vata and settled them
<>there. They were put up there in a palace specially [Page129-b+ 64]
<>made of lac. The Pa1n2d2avas divined the secret of it and
<>escaped from the fire, when the palace was set fire to.
<>Verse 10, Chapter 147 of the A1di Parva states that it
<>was Bhi1ma, who set fire to the palace. Escaping thus
<>through a tunnel the Pa1n2d2avas travelled a great distance
<>in the forest. Kunti1 and four of her sons got tired by the
<>exertions of the travel and were forced to sit down for
<>rest on the way. Bhi1ma, continued the journey carrying
<>the mother and his four brothers on his shoulders. With
<>their entry into Hid2im3ba forest the weakness left them,
<>and they became their former selves.
<NI>4) {%Hid2im3ba killed.%} Kunti1 devi1 and four sons slept under
<>the shade of a tree at dusk, and Bhi1ma kept guard over
<>them. There dwelt in the forest a Ra1ks2asa called Hid2im3ba
<>with his sister, Hid2im3bi1. Hid2im3ba looked around that
<>particular day from the top of a tree, and detecting
<>Bhi1ma his mouth watered. He deputed Hid2imbi1 to
<>bring Bhi1ma over to him. Hid2im3bi1 approached Bhi1ma,
<>whose fine figure kindled feelings of love in her. She
<>desired to have him as husband. Hid2im3bi1 having not
<>returned even after a long time Hidim3ba went over to
<>the spot, and there finding Hid2im3bi1 in love-talks with
<>Bhi1ma he got terribly angry. He wanted to kill Hid2im3bi1.
<>Bhi1ma, who could not suffer the killing of a woman in

<NI>2) {%Birth and Boyhood.%} Bhi1s2ma's name in his boyhood was
<>Devavrata. He was the eighth son of S4antanu, a king

<>S4antanu, his father was the re-birth of another king,

<NI>King Maha1bhis2eka after his death, attained Vis2n2uloka.
<>Once he went to visit Brahma1 at Satyaloka. At that
<>time Gan3ga1devi1 was also present in Brahma1's assembly.
<>In that pious atmosphere, a gentle breeze began to blow
<>and Gan3ga1devi1's clothes were slightly deranged. Just

<>come to the earth to be born as her sons and that after-
<>wards she could come back to Heaven. After that
<>Gan3ga1devi1 was born as a mortal woman in the world
<>under the name Gan3ga1 and she spent her days in the
<>forests near the Gan3ga1 river valleys.
<NI>In those days the ruler of the Lunar dynasty was a king
<>named Prati1pa. Having no children, he went to the

<>Gan3ga1devi1 who was moving about in the forests near-
<>by, saw the King deeply absorbed in his tapas. She
<>approached him and sat on his right thigh. She wanted
<>the King to be her husband. He explained to her that
<>the right thigh is the proper seat of a daughter-in-law [Page135-a+ 65]
<>and so she would become his son's wife in due course.
<>In course of time, Prati1pa had a son, S4antanu, born
<>to him. When S4antanu grew up into a young man, one

<NI>At about that time, the wife of Dyo, one of the As2t2a-
<>vasus, happened to see the sacrificial cow of the sage

<NI>Gan3ga1devi1 became pregnant and gave birth to her first

<NI>Seven children were born to her and she threw all of them

<NI>3) {%The name Bhi1s2ma.%} Devavrata was anointed, as
<>heir-apparent. One day King S4antanu reached the
<>forest near the Gan3ga1 river valley, for hunting. As he

<F>1) Satyavati1's original name was Ka1li1. The fisherman got her from the stomach of a fish. (See the word Adrika1). Since she
<>had the smell of fish she got the name of “Matsyagandhi1.” She used to assist a fisherman in his work as a ferryman in the river Gan3ga1.
<>Once the sage Para1s4ara happened to get into her boat and he fell deeply in love with her. The sage removed the smell of fish from her and gave
<>her the perfume of musk instead. By this mystic power he created a mist at noon and under its cover, he had a sexual union with her. As
<>a result of it the child Kr2s2n2a (Vya1sa) was born. The child immediately left the mother to perform tapas in the forest after promising to
<>return to her whenever she wished for his presence. Although she gave birth to a child, Para1s4ara blessed that she would again remain a
<>virgin. The whole episode remained a secret. As usual, Satyavati1 returned to the fisherman's cottage in the evening and continued to
<>live with him. It is at this stage that S4antanu was attracted by the perfume of musk and came to the cottage where he met Satyavati1.</F> The king
<>fell in love with her at first sight. He asked the fisherman
<>to give the girl in marriage to him. But the brave fisher- [Page135-b+ 57]
<>man did not yield to the king's demand immediately.
<>He laid down several conditions, one of which was that
<>Satyavati1's sons should succeed to the throne of S4antanu.
<>The king was in a fix. Devavrata was the eldest son and
<>heir-apparent. To deny kingship to his sons would be

<NI>When Devavrata knew about his father's condition, he

<HI>BHU1TAS. (A set of beings created by Rudra).

<HI>BODHISATTVA. A good-natured husband generally
<>quoted in Sanskrit works. The following is the story

<NI>Once there lived a wealthy Vais4ya, who had a son named
<>Bodhisattva. When the childhood of the boy was at an

<>his son also married. Because of the ear-buzzing of his

<>sattva left the house of his father, with his wife. By

<>sandy place with nothing else in sight. He walked for
<>seven days carrying his wife on his shoulders. His wife
<>grew weary and worn with hunger and thirst. Seeing

<>The wicked woman took them and saved herself from
<>death. On the eighth day they reached the jungles of a
<>hilly place full of fruit-trees and with a river with grassy
<>banks, flowing down to the valley. With fruits and cool
<>water he appeased the hunger and thirst of his wife.
<>Then he got down to the river to take a bath. He saw
<>a man with his limbs cut off, coming afloat. Now and
<>then he was producing pitiable sounds. The kind son of
<>the Vais4ya, without minding his weakness due to fast for
<>the last seven days, swam to the man and brought him to
<>the bank of the river. He did all services possible for him.
<>Then he asked him who had cut off his limbs. He rep-
<>lied that his enemies had done so, with the intention that
<>he might die suffering severe pain for a long time. The
<>Vais4ya's son stood still for a little while. Then he took
<>his bath. With his wife he lived in the forest doing
<>penance. The wounds of the man he saved had been
<>healed. The Vais4ya's son, one day, went out to the
<>forest to gather fruits and roots for their food. At that
<>time his wife grew lustful and had coition with the man
<>without limbs. Gradually she began to dote on him. She
<>decided to kill her husband who was an impediment on
<>her way. She pretended to be ill. The Vais4ya's son began
<>to treat her. One day she took her husband to the edge of
<>a very deep well and said: “See, there is a divine herb at
<>the bottom of this well. I will be cured if I could eat it.
<>This is what a goddess told me in a dream yesternight”.
<>Hearing this her husband made a rope, and tied it to a
<>tree. Then he began to go down the well by the rope.
<>She cut the rope and the man fell into the well. There
<>was a passage from the well to the river. The current
<>took him through that passage to the river. He got out of
<>the river, and sat under a tree thinking of the wickedness
<>of women. There was a city close by. At that time the
<>King of the city was dead and there was no heir left. The
<>subjects of the city brought an elephant and said, “whom
<>ever this elephant takes and places on his back shall be
<>our king”. They sent the elephant out. The elephant [Page147-a+ 64]
<>was pleased at the virtuous character of the son of the
<>Vais4ya. So taking him, as if he was God, placed him on
<>its back and walked to the city. The people gathered
<>round him and anointed him as their King. The son of
<>the Vais4ya became King. He never even thought of
<>women who are generally fickle and wicked.
<NI>The wicked wife of the Vais4ya's son took the limbless
<>man on her shoulder and wandered about saying, “The
<>enemies of my husband have put him in this plight.
<>Because of my conjugal fidelity I carry him thus and
<>earn our daily bread. Please give us alms”. In this
<>manner she spent her days in begging. Thus wandering
<>from place to place she reached the city where the
<>Vaisya's son was the King. The people, seeing her

<NI>1) Inside what atom which is unit and multiple at the

<NI>2) What does shine as ether and non-ether?
<NI>3) What is it that is something and nothing?
<NI>4) What is it that is going and not going at the same

<NI>5) What is it that has taken form from voidness?
<NI>6) What is it that is moving and at the same time station-

<NI>7) Who draws pictures in clear sky?
<NI>8) In what seed do the worlds exist as a big tree in its

<NI>9) From what substance can the living and non-living

<>below in the order of the questions.
<NI>1) Hey, Giantess: All the questions you have put be-
<>fore us encased in figurative words discernible only to
<>the Vedic sages, are concerned with the supreme Being.
<>The atom is the supreme Spirit which is beyond all
<>knowledge of the mind and the senses. As it is without
<>organs of action it is as unmanifested as the sky. And
<>inside that supreme atom which could be felt only by the
<>mind, crores and crores of bubbles of universes originate
<>and vanish due to frailty.
<NI>2) The impersonal Supreme Being, having no substance,
<>pervades everything. This Supreme Being, Brahman,
<>is pure knowledge (Jn5a1nasvaru1pa). It is the sky and the
<>non-sky.
<NI>3) As it is indescribable the Impersonal Supreme Spirit
<>is nothing, but as it is a reality it is something.
<NI>4) As it pervades everything accessible, the Impersonal
<>Supreme Spirit has the quality of motion. But as it has
<>no emotions and as there exists no space beyond, it is
<>motionless.
<NI>5) As it is inaccessible to others the Supreme Spirit is
<>having no existence, but as it is the essence of everything
<>that is good, it has existence.
<NI>6) The Supreme Spirit is the radiance of motion or
<>activity and as there is nothing else to be found out, that
<>is, as it doesn't know anything else it is as rigid as a
<>rock.
<NI>7) In the clear sky the Supreme Spirit draws the pictures
<>of the universe.
<NI>8) Exists in the Supreme Atom. [Page152-b+ 65]
<NI>9) As the entire visible world cannot be separated from
<>the Supreme Spirit nothing is other than the Impersonal
<>Supreme Spirit.
<NI>10) The differentiations of the various worlds are mere
<>appearances of the Supreme Spirit and so dualism is of the
<>same figure.
<NI>The King drew Karkkat2i1 nearer to the Impersonal
<>Supreme Spirit. He advised her not to commit slaughter.

<>She asked, what could he offer to a giantess as food.

<NI>14) {%The age of Brahma1.%} Forty-three crores twenty lacs
<>of human years is one four-yuga period called ‘Deva-

<>One thousand deva caturyugas will make one Maha1yuga
<>(great yuga) A Maha1yuga is a day time of Brahma1.
<>During the period of one Maha1yuga, that is, during
<>one day of Brahma1, fourteen Manus, one after another,
<>help Brahma1 in doing the work of creation. This is the
<>time of the seventh Manu in the present day time
<>(Kalpa) of the present Brahma1. The period of six Manus
<>are over in the present day time of the present Brahma1.
<>Vaivasvata is the present Manu. Brahma1 wakes up in
<>the morning--the beginning of a Kalpa. Those which
<>underwent destruction in the night, are created again
<>in the morning. As Brahma1 wakes up daily in the morn-
<>ing, what are the things created before, which do not

<>without destruction, six or twentyfour tattvas (princi-
<>ples) which are natural creations. These twenty-four
<>principles are not the creation of Brahma1. He who is
<>beyond names, He who created Brahma1 in the lotus
<>flower, created them. Brahma1 who was originated in the

<>ples. The work of creation performed by Brahma1 is
<>called Pratisarga (substitute creation). Everything
<>Brahma1 created in the day time will be destroyed in the

<NI>15) {%The creations and substitute creations of Brahma1.%} The
<>creations performed by Brahma1 are of two kinds. The

<HI>BRAHMA. See Parabrahma.
<HI>BRA1HMA. A kind of marriage. The bride is adorn-
<>ed with all kinds of ornaments and is taken to bride-
<>groom; and given to him as wife. This is called Bra1hma
<>marriage. Maha1bha1rata, A1di Parva, Chapter 73,
<>Stanza 8 states that this mode of marriage was allowed
<>to all the four castes of ancient Bha1rata.
<HI>BRAHMABALI. An individual of a dynasty of teachers.
<>(See Guruparam3para1).
<HI>BRAHMACA1RI I. See Brahmacarya.
<HI>BRAHMACA1RI II. A devagandharva (a class of Gods)
<>born to Kas4yapapraja1pati of his wife Pr2tha1. He took
<>part in the Birth festival of Arjuna. (M.B. A1di Parva,
<>Chapters 65 and 122).
<HI>BRAHMACARYA. In ancient India an ideal life was
<>considered to pass through four stages, and Brahma-
<>carya is one of the stages of life. The four stages
<>are Brahmacarya (Vedic student vowed to chastity),
<>Ga1rhasthya (married householder), Va1naprastha (forest
<>hermit) and Sannya1sa (an ascetic who has renounced
<>the world). Brahmacarya, the first stage of the four
<>is considered as the period of education. The rules and
<>conduct of a Brahmaca1ri1 are given in Manusmr2ti,
<>Chapter 2.
<NI>The brahmaca1ri1 who lives with the teacher has to obey
<>certain rules and principles. He should bathe in the
<>river at sun-rise and offer oblations to gods and manes.
<>A brahmaca1ri1 has to abstain from using honey, meat,
<>fragrance, flowers, flower of chrysanthemum (Ind.)
<>women, curd, milk, ghee, churned-curd, slaughter,
<>bath applying oil, anointing the eyes with collyrium,
<>sandals, umbrella, lust, anger, covetousness, dance,
<>music, gambling, slander, ridicule, falsehood, and
<>causing injury to others. A Brahmaca1ri1 should go to
<>bed alone. Semen should not be made to discharge
<>through lust. If seminal discharge occurs in dream he
<>should take bath early in the morning and worship the
<>Sun, pronouncing the mantra or spell ‘Punah2’ thrice.
<>The Brahmaca1ri1 should live on alms. It is the duty of
<>the brahmaca1ri1 to bring water, flower for oblation,
<>cowdung, soil and darbha (grass) for the teacher. He
<>should receive alms only from the houses of those who
<>believe in the Vedas and sacrifices. He should not go
<>to the house of his teacher or his heirs and their families
<>for alms. Provided there are no other houses he may
<>receive alms from the houses of his teacher's relatives
<>and in the absence of such houses he may approach
<>the houses of heirs to his teacher and in the absence
<>of such houses he may receive alms from the house of
<>the teacher. He should fetch ‘Camata’ (fuel chiefly
<>from butea frondosa) from a place of purity in the [Page156-a+ 65]
<>forest, as instructed in rules and dry it in the sun; in
<>the absence of which it may be got dried in a sheltered
<>place. This fuel should be put in the sacrificial fire in
<>the mornings, at noons, and in the evenings. If a healthy
<>Brahmaca1ri1 fails in doing his duties consecutively for
<>seven days it will be considered that his vow of Brahma-
<>carya is broken and then he will have to take the vow
<>of ‘Avaki1rn2i’ again. Without waiting for the order of
<>the teacher, the Brahmaca1ri1 (student) should engage
<>himself in devotion and meditation and in the service
<>of the teacher daily. When the student is before the
<>teacher he should stand with folded hands controlling
<>his body, speech, brains, sensitive organs, and mind.
<>Only when he is asked to sit, should he do so before
<>the teacher, covering the portions of his body, which
<>are to be covered, with clothes. He should rise up in
<>the morning before his teacher wakes up, and go to
<>bed only after the teacher has retired for sleep. When
<>his teacher calls him, he should not give reply lying,
<>sitting, walking, eating or looking in the opposite
<>direction. He should not gainsay the teacher. The
<>student should attend to the orders of the teacher and
<>comply with them, sitting if the teacher is sitting,
<>standing if the teacher is standing, standing back if the
<>teacher is advancing towards him, running behind if
<>he is walking, standing close by when he is facing the
<>opposite direction, folding his limbs when the teacher
<>is lying or sitting near. The student should have his
<>seat and bed one step lower than those of his teacher.
<>The student should not sit in a careless manner in
<>places where the teacher's eyes could reaeh. He should
<>not utter the name of his teacher. If anybody speaks ill
<>of his teacher he should close his ears and run away
<>from the spot. If a Brahmaca1ri1 scoffs his teacher, he
<>will be born as a donkey, and as a dog if he scorns him,
<>and as a worm if he steals the wealth of his teacher
<>and as a beetle if he becomes jealous at the greatness
<>of his teacher. When the teacher is angry the brahma-
<>ca1ri1 should not go near him. The Brahmaca1ri1 should
<>not speak unasked. A Brahmaca1ri1 could sit with his
<>teacher only when they are in a vehicle, or on a camel
<>or in a tower or on the steps or on rocks or in a boat. He
<>should consider the teacher of his teacher as his teacher.
<>He should not address his parents who visit the house
<>of the teacher, without the permission of his teacher. He
<>should respect learned men, holymen, sons of the
<>teacher and those who are born of his family, as a
<>teacher. If the wife of the teacher is of the caste of the
<>teacher, the brahmaca1ri1 should consider her as his
<>teacher. If the wife is not of the same caste the brahma-
<>ca1ri1 needs only to stand up and make obeisance to her.
<>A brahmaca1ri1 should not apply oil to the body of his
<>teacher's wife, wash her, massage her body, and comb
<>her hair. A brahmaca1ri1 may either shave his head or
<>grow matted hair. He should never be asleep at sunrise
<>or sunset. For learning Vedas etc. the student should not
<>give the teacher cows, clothes etc. as free gifts before-
<>hand. On completion of education, when the student
<>asks the teacher for permission to get married, he should
<>give the teacher what he demands. A brahmaca1ri1 who
<>has fully complied with the rules mentioned above,
<>will attain heaven after his death.

<HI>BRAHMA1N2D2A. The word Brahma1n2d2a means the an2d2a
<>of Brahma1 (an2d2a-egg), the Supreme Being which is
<>the root of the origin of the universe. At a time long
<>ago, which is beyond reckoning, there was nothing but
<>an egg. This egg was split into two and from it a male [Page159-a+ 64]

<>cried for a while, because of hunger and thirst. He

<>from Brahma1) by those versed in the Pura1n2as. The
<>boy was so called because he was the most material
<>of materiality. But he was an atom of atoms and the
<>first figuration of God. From each pore of the skin of
<>the great vira1t2, who was the base of all the worlds a
<>universe came into being. Thus all the countless uni-
<>verses were born. Each universe has its own trinity of
<>Brahma1, Vis2n2u, S4iva and devas (the bright ones), the
<>protectors of the eight zones. One universe comprises
<>fourteen worlds or realms, from Pa1ta1la to the Brahma-
<>loka (from the nether world to the upper world or
<>the realm of Brahma1). Countless such universes exist.
<>Over and above all these universes there is Vaikun2t2ha,
<>and above Vaikun2t2ha there is another world with an
<>area of fifty crore yojanas (leagues), called ‘Goloka’ (the
<>world of cow). Only the two worlds Vaikun2t2ha and
<>the Goloka are eternal. Bhu1loka (the earth) consists
<>of seven islands and sixty-four peninsulas. There are
<>seven worlds above and seven worlds below. The seven
<>upper worlds are Bhu1loka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Jana-
<>loka, Tapoloka. Satyaloka and Brahmaloka. Thus a
<>universe consists of fourteen worlds. This is the idea
<>given by the Pura1n2as about Brahma1n2d2a. (Devi1 Bha1ga-
<>vata, Skandhas 9).
<NI>Mention is made, in the Vis2n2u Pura1n2a, Am3s4a 2,
<>Chapter 7, about the construction of Brahma1n2d2a.
<NI>This Brahma1n2d2a, like the seed of the Kapittha tree
<>(Vitar--the wood-apple), is covered under, above and
<>all around by an2d2akat2a1ha (egg-shell). The an2d2a (egg)
<>is covered by water ten times the egg in volume. This
<>water-shell is covered by a shell of fire. Around the
<>shell of fire there is the shell of air and the air-shell
<>is covered with ether. Around the shell of ether there
<>is the shell of Egoism of darkness. Over the shell of
<>Egoism there is the shell of glory and the shell of
<>glory is covered by Prakr2ti, the Divine Nature. It is
<>immeasurable. Prakr2ti contains numberless Brah-
<>ma1n2d2as. As oil exists in sesame, God pervades the whole
<>universe. This is the connection between Prakr2ti and
<>Purus2a. (The Nature and the Supreme Spirit).

<HI>BUDDHA. The founder of Buddhism. Some consider

<NI>The story given above is in accordance with the Pura1-
<>n2as. The following are the facts gained by historic
<>investigations.
<NI>Gautama Buddha was born in B.C. 560, in Kapilavastu
<>near the Hima1layas. His father was S4uddhodana. He
<>was born in the family of the S4a1kyas. The word ‘S4a1kya’
<>is another form of the word Ks2atriya. The real name of
<>Buddha was Siddha1rtha. S4uddhodana brought up his
<>son in such a way that he should not be subjected to
<>any sort of mental pain or worry. So he kept Buddha
<>aloof from the outer world. Thus he spent his childhood
<>in comfort and pleasure. Once by chance he happened
<>to see a sick man, an old man and a dead body. The
<>sight made him thoughtful. He began to think upon
<>a way to remove sorrow and pain from the world and
<>to bring about peace and comfort.
<NI>The change that appeared in the son worried the
<>father. So at the age of sixteen he made Siddha1rtha
<>marry Yas4odhara1. A son was born to them. But the
<>mind of Siddha1rtha was restless, distressed and agi-
<>tated. One day Siddha1rtha discarded everything and
<>went out of the palace alone.
<NI>Siddha1rtha wandered from place to place learning
<>from various teachers. But he did not find peace.
<>Once on a full-moon day while he was sitting in medi-
<>tation under a banian tree he got ‘Bodha’. (insight or
<>conviction). From that day onwards he began to be
<>known by the name ‘Buddha’. After that he came to
<>Ka1s4i, and told his disciples how he got Bodha or con-
<>viction. The number of his followers increased day by
<>day. Thus Buddhism came into being. Buddha said
<>that the reason for pain and sorrow in the world was
<>desire and that sorrow could be exterminated only
<>by controlling and overcoming all desire. To attain
<>Eternal Bliss one should be true and righteous in
<>thought, deed and word and that ‘Not Killing’ was
<>the foundation of righteousness. Buddhism spread
<>everywhere in Bha1rata.
<NI>Gautama Buddha died at the age of eighty.

<HI>BUDDHISM. (BUDDHA-MATA). The origin of Bud-
<>dhism was in the sixth century B.C. This new religion
<>was shaped out of Hinduism that prevailed at that
<>time. Buddhism which had its origin in North India,
<>prevailed everywhere in India up to the eleventh [Page166-a+ 65]
<>century A.D. During that period there was an over-
<>flow of this religion to the other parts of Asia. Now
<>this religion has its full sway over the people of Burma.
<>90% of the population there, are adherents of Bud-
<>dhism. 80% of the people of Thailand, 60% of the
<>people in Ceylon and Japan and 17% in China are
<>now Buddhists. In India, Pakistan and the Philippines
<>the Buddhists are only a minority. Even though Indo-
<>nesia is a Muslim country there is a small class of
<>Buddhists there. Combodia, Lavos and Tibet are consi-
<>dered to be Buddhist countries. In Nepal there are
<>only two religions, Hinduism and Buddhism. In count-
<>ries outside Asia there are followers of Buddhism.
<>Statistics reveal that there are one hundred and sixty-
<>five thousand Buddhists in North America, one
<>hundred and thirtyfive thousand in South America,
<>and ten thousand in Europe. The number of Buddhists
<>in the world today is 150.31 crores.

<HI>CA1KYA1RKU1TTU. A very important art practised in
<>temples mainly in Kerala. It is called so because it is
<>exhibited by Ca1kya1rs (a sect attached to temples). In
<>important temples a place called Ku1ttambala is set
<>apart for displaying the art. The Ku1ttu now prevalent
<>in Kerala temples is not exactly of its old form. Kula-
<>s4ekharavarma1 peruma1l (elected ruler of old Kerala)
<>effected some changes in the old art form, and Bha1skara-
<>ravivarma1 peruma1l and Tolakavi made further reforms
<>in it. The art of Ku1ttu was evolved with the object of
<>relating pura1n2ic stories in such a manner as will help
<>devotional feelings grow in man.
<NI>The main aim of the Ku1ttu is to narrate pura1n2ic
<>stories in such a way as to instil Bhakti in the hearers
<>and to create an interest in them in the Pura1n2as. The
<>Ca1kya1r (the man who gives the discourse who usually
<>belongs to the Brahmin sect called Ca1kya1rs) tells the
<>story in a very interesting way, reciting appropriate
<>passages from the Pura1n2as and illustrating them with
<>apt examples and similes. The narration is from the
<>beginning till end humorous. The Ca1kya1r who delivers
<>the discourse is usually a man with a good sense of
<>humour and a sense of what is odd, strange or eccentric
<>in nature and human character. There are three varie- [Page168-a+ 65]
<>ties of Ku1ttu: Prabandham3 Ku1ttu, Nam3biar Ku1ttu and
<>Ku1t2ia1t2t2am. Of these the first is narrative (A1khya1na-
<>para) while in the second and third type, the element
<>of acting is more important (Abhinayapara).

<HI>CA1N2AKYA (KAUT2ILYA). The famous author of
<>“Arthas4a1stra” a treatise on political economy.
<NI>Eastern and western scholars have made exhaustive
<>researches on this intellectual giant of ancient India,
<>Ca1n2akya. But, nothing definite has yet been established
<>about his time or life. Indians have accepted as a fact
<>the traditional legend that he was a minister of Candra-
<>gupta, the founder of the Maurya dynasty. It is also
<>firmly believed that it was this mighty intellect of a
<>brahmin who made Candragupta a powerful emperor
<>and steered the ship of his state. The phrase ‘Ca1n2akya's
<>kut2ilani1ti’ (crooked tactics) has become proverbial.
<>Some scholars hold the opinion that he came to be
<>called ‘Kaut2ilya’ because of his Kut2ila (crooked)
<>tactics; but evidence to establish this view-point is yet
<>to be adduced.
<NI>It is his famous Arthas4a1stra, which has made Ca1n2akya's
<>name a world famous one. The great German thinker
<>Jolly has described the Arthas4a1stra as a unique composi-
<>tion in the Sanskrit language. And, Johann Meyer, the
<>great western scholar has the following to say about
<>the book:--
<NI>“Kaut2ilya's Arthas4a1stra is not one single text, it is a
<>collection and collateration of all books in ancient
<>India. To study the greatness of the theories and
<>principles contained in it today requires continuous and
<>constant study at least for twenty years and the un-
<>remitting efforts of a scholar with unabounded know-
<>ledge are required.” [Page169-a+ 65]
<>Even his name has not yet been confirmed beyond
<>doubts. Kaut2ilya is also called Vis2n2ugupta, Ca1n2akya,
<>Dramila, and An3gula. Modern researches place the
<>date of the Arthas4a1stra at near about B.C. 400. In
<>Vis4a1khadatta's Mudra1ra1ksasa (drama) the name
<>Kaut2ilya is used.
<NI>The Authors of Ni1tis4a1stra maintain that the name of
<>the author of Arthas4a1stra was Vis2n2ugupta. It may be
<>gathered from the Mudra1ra1ks2asa that he became famous
<>as Ca1n2akya as he was the son of Can2aka, and that
<>he possessed deep erudition in Ni1tis4a1stra, Dharma-
<>s4a1stra and astrology. There is another legend to the
<>effect that this brahmin (Ca1n2akya) belonged to Ka1n5ci1-
<>pura and that he migrated to Pa1t2ali1putra, the seat of
<>learning and scholarship. As Ka1mandaka, who lived
<>in the fourth century B.C. has eulogised Ca1n2akya in
<>his ni1tis4a1stra it may be surmised that Ca1n2akya lived
<>sometime near about that. Candragupta and Ca1n2akya
<>are referred to in the Vis2n2u and the Va1mana Pura1n2as.
<>Kaut2ilya was keen-eyed and scholar par excellence.
<>“Arthas4a1stra” is a great book written by him after
<>thoroughly examining the viewpoints of previous
<>scholars, and then establishing his own views and
<>theories. From the Das4akuma1racarita of Dan2d2i1 (A.D.
<>700) it may be seen that there are 6000 verses in the
<>Anus2t2up metre (eight letters in one line) in the Artha-
<>s4a1stra composed by Vis2n2ugupta for the use of Candra-
<>gupta Maurya. The Artha a1stra has been held in praise
<>by Ba1n2abhat2t2a who lived in the 7th Century, Soma-
<>devasu1ri, who lived in the 10th century and also by
<>Hemacandra, the author of Ka1vya1nus4a1sana, who lived
<>in the 12th century. The book is a discourse on the
<>principles and practices that are necessary to establish
<>a strong government of an ideal empire. Ca1n2akya has
<>mentioned in his book with respect the old scholars like
<>Manu, S4ukra, Br2haspati, Na1ra1yan2a, Ka1tya1yana and
<>Govinda di1ks2ita. (For the pura1n2ic story about Ca1n2akya
<>see Vararuci, Para 6).

<HI>CATURIKA1. A harlot about whom the following story

<HI>CATURUPA1YAM. The four means used by Kings in
<>olden times to achieve their objects are called Caturu-
<>pa1yam. Sa1ma, da1na, bheda and dan2d2a are the Catur-
<>upa1yas (four tactics). There are three other upa1yas
<>also, almost equally important as the first four, and the
<>seven upa1yas are collectively called Saptopa1yas. There
<>are also yet other upa1yas, but they are not important
<>enough to merit special mention.
<NI>1) {%Sa1ma.%} It is the best means to attract and convert
<>others to one's side. It consists in winning people with
<>sweet words and looks. People who are friendly by
<>temperament and straightforward may be brought
<>round by sa1ma. Sa1ma is employed in dealing with sons,
<>brothers and other relatives.
<NI>2) {%Da1na.%} There are five kinds or varieties of da1na
<>(gift) viz. pri1tida1na, dravyada1na, svayam3gra1ha, deya
<>and pratimoks2a. If a person gets help from another
<>and acknowledges help by reward that reward is
<>called pri1tida1na. The miser and the poor should be
<>brought round by pri1tida1na. Military captains, heroes
<>and citizens should be won over by this da1na. Those
<>who fall at feet should be honoured by da1na.
<NI>3) {%Bheda.%} Bhedopa1ya is of three kinds: to destroy or
<>end the friendship subsisting between people, to create
<>dissension and to make the parties quarrel with each
<>other. He who is falsely praised, he who does not desire
<>wealth or welfare, he who has been invited to come and
<>then insulted, traitor to king, he who has been exorbi-
<>tantly taxed, the angry one, the honourable one, the
<>insulted, the unreasonably forsaken one, he who har-
<>bours hatred in his mind, the pacified one, one whose
<>wealth and wife have been taken away or stolen, he
<>who has not been respected though deserving of respect--
<>if such people are in one's opposite camp, suspicion
<>should be raked up among them and thus division crea-
<>ted in their ranks. If subordinate chieftains, and forest
<>tribes commit offences they should be brought round
<>by the use of sa1ma and bheda upa1yas.
<NI>4) {%Dan2d2a.%} Dan2d2opa1ya is of three kinds, viz, killing,
<>denuding of wealth, and inflicting pain on the body or
<>torture. Dan2d2a has two other forms, praka1s4a (open)
<>and apraka1s4a (secret). Those who have become objects
<>of hatred to all people should be subjected to praka1s4a-
<>dan2d2a. People, whose killing the world will detest,
<>should not be killed openly, but only secretly. Enemies
<>should be killed with weapons etc. Brahmins should not
<>be killed. Friends and allies should not be subjected
<>to dan2d2a; friends, who are made objects of dan2d2a will
<>wither away like worm-eaten trees. The King, who
<>possesses the three powers (of wealth, army and people's
<>support) and is fully conscious of the time and environ-
<>mental factors should annihilate enemies by the instru-
<>ment of dan2d2a. Evil people should be defeated by
<>dan2d2a itself.
<NI>The upa1ya ma1ya1 consists in practising deception by
<>magic or other yogic powers. The powers can be
<>acquired by the worship of the idols of certain Devata1s.
<>People who employ go about at night in various dis-
<>guises. They disguise themselves as beautiful women or
<>even as animals. They also deceive people by creating
<>illusions of clouds, fire or lightning. For instance, Bhi1ma
<>killed Ki1caka by going to him in the guise of a woman. [Page180-a+ 65]
<>Not to dissuade people who indulge in unjustifiable
<>grief, war etc. is the principal aim of the upa1ya called
<>upeks2a1. Hid2imbi1 gave up his brother Hidimba by
<>practising Upeks2a1. Next is the Indraja1lopa1ya (magic).
<>For example, to create illusions of clouds, darkness, rain,
<>fire, and other magic in order to instil fear among
<>troops of the enemy etc. To scare the enemy is the aim
<>of Indraja1la. (For details of Caturupa1yas see Kan2ika).
<>(Agni Pura1n2a, Chapter 241).
<HI>CA1TURVARN2YAM. (The four Castes, Classes).
<NI>1) {%General.%} The pura1n2as tell that Brahma1 created the
<>four castes like Brahmins, Ks2atriyas, Vais4yas and S4u1dras
<>and assigned to them duties and rules of procedure.
<NI>2) {%Origin.%} Brahma1 got ready for the work of Crea-
<>tion, concentrating his mind on the universal soul, the
<>embodiment of Truth. And, the first to be born from his
<>face were people with sublime qualities, and them he
<>called Brahmins. Then emerged from his chest people
<>in whom the heroic or militant qualities preponderated.
<>(Ra1jasa). Them the Creator named Ks2atriyas. Then
<>from his thighs were born people in whom rajas and
<>tamas preponderated, and they were called Vais4yas.
<>And, lastly Brahma1 brought forth from his feet another
<>sect of people, and as tamas (darkness, cultural darkness)
<>preponderated in them they were named S4u1dras. The
<>system of four castes is called Ca1turvarn2yam. (Vis2n2u
<>Pura1n2a, Part 1, Chapter 6).
<NI>3) {%Code of conduct.%} Ahim3sa1 (non-violence), Satyava1da
<>(speaking truth), Bhu1tada1ya (love for all living beings),
<>Ti1rthaseva1 (resort to holy places), Da1na (gifts), Brahma-
<>carya (celibacy), Vimatsaratva (absence of malice),
<>Service of Devas, Brahmins and Gurus (elders), to attend
<>to all dharmas (duties), Pitr2pu1ja1 (worship of elders)
<>eternal loyalty to King, to accomplish objects in con-
<>formity with the injunction of the S4a1stras, not to commit
<>cruel deeds, Titiks2a1 (forbearance, to put up with
<>equanimity the pair of opposites such as pleasure and
<>pain, heat and cold), belief in God--these codes of con-
<>duct are common to all Castes and in all the four stations
<>in life. Now, the special codes for each of the four
<>castes.
<NI>1) {%Brahmins.%} To perform and get performed Yajn5as,
<>to study and to teach the Vedas, to give gifts and to
<>receive gifts--these form the dharma (duties) of the
<>Brahmin. Brahmins take their second birth (dvija)
<>on the upanayana (wearing of the sacred thread).
<>The caste of the mother is the caste of the child. But
<>children born to Brahmins of their non-Brahmin wives
<>are not Brahmins. Children born of a Brahmin woman
<>to a S4u1dra1 are called Can2d2a1las. Sons born of Brahmin
<>women to Ks2atriyas are called Su1tas, and sons born of a
<>Brahmin woman to a Vais4ya are called Vaidehikas.
<>The Brahmin shall not adopt the profession of the other
<>castes. The twice-born are, however, allowed in certain
<>circumstances, the profession of agriculture, protection
<>of cows, commerce and kusi1da (to lend money on inte-
<>rest). But, he shall not trade in gorasa (milk and other
<>cow products) lavan2a (salt) and flesh. If he be an
<>agriculturist, the Brahmin may till the earth, cut medi-
<>cinal plants and destroy pests. But, he must purify the
<>soul by performing yajn5as and worshipping Devas.
<>The soil should be ploughed with eight oxen attached to
<>the plough. He may sustain himself either with R2ta
<>(food got by begging) or Amr2ta (food got not by beg-
<>ging). The suffix “S4arma1” should be added to the names [Page180-b+ 64]
<>of Brahmin children. Upanayana (wearing of the sacred
<>thread) should be done when the child is eight years
<>old. The maun5ji (girdle around the waist) to be worn
<>after upanayana should be made either of mun5ja grass
<>or of the bark of trees. Brahmin brahmaca1rins should
<>wear hides, and when they beg for alms the sentence
<>should commence with the word ‘Bhavati’, e.g. “Bhavati,
<>bhiks2a1m3 dehi). The Brahmin can marry in all the castes,
<>but he shall perform ritual only along with the wife of
<>his own caste.
<NI>{%ii) Ks2atriya.%} To give gifts according to rules, study
<>Vedas and perform yajn5as form the duty of the Ks2atriya.
<>To look after and take care of good people and to punish
<>evil-doers are his especial duties. Names of Ks2atriya
<>children should take the suffix “Varma1”. After upana-
<>yana the child should wear tiger skin. He should carry
<>a dan2d2a (rod) of the Araya1l (peepal) tree. When the
<>Ks2atriya brahmaca1rin begs for alms the word ‘bhavati’
<>should be used in the middle of the sentence, e.g. “Bhiks2a1m3
<>bhavati dehi”. The Ks2atriya can marry in the other
<>castes, except the Brahmin. At the time of wedding the
<>Ks2atriya woman should hold an arrow in her hand.
<NI>{%iii) Vais4ya.%} Agriculture, protection of cows and trade
<>are the special duties of the Vais4ya. Children born of
<>Brahmin women to Vais4yas are called Vaidehikas.
<>Names of Vais4ya children should have the suffix ‘gupta’
<>after them. After upanayana the Vais4ya brahmaca1rin
<>should wear sheep's skin. He should carry a dan2d2a made
<>of a branch of the Ku1vala tree. The Vais4ya may have a
<>wife of his own caste and one of the S4u1dra caste. At
<>the time of wedding the Vais4ya woman should hold a
<>cane in her hand.
<NI>{%iv) S4u1dra.%} Service to the Brahmin and architecture
<>form the duties of the S4u1dra. Children born to Ks2atriya
<>women by S4u1dras are called Pulkasas. Children born
<>to Brahmin women by S4u1dras are called Can2d2a1las,
<>and sons born to S4u1dras by Vais4ya women are called
<>A1yogavas.
<NI>The Can2d2a1la's profession is to hang criminals sentenced
<>to death, and to live by women. The Pulkasa must
<>live by hunting. A1yogava is to act on the stage and live
<>by architecture. The Can2d2a1la should live outside the
<>village. The Can2d2a1la has a right to take the clothes on
<>corpses. He shall not have any physical contacts with
<>the others. He will attain salvation if he died in the
<>course of protecting others. The suffix ‘da1sa’ should be
<>added to his name. He shall marry only from his own
<>caste. (Agni Pura1n2a, 4 Chapters from 151).

<HI>CA1VET2T2UPAT2A. (CA1VERU). (Pat2a = army).
<NI>A particular division of the army which in olden days
<>used to come forward to lay down their lives in the
<>service of the country. When defeat in war was almost
<>certain for their king an army division under royal [Page181-a+ 64]
<>leadership was formed of heroes, who took their last
<>leave of their homes and people. The soldiers left their
<>homes with their head and eyebrows shaved, and people
<>gave them a hearty send-off. Either victory or death
<>in battlefield was their slogan. This system originated
<>in Kerala. Imitating Kerala, Turkey and Egypt formed
<>their own division of Ca1vet2t2upat2a in the 15th century.
<>The Ca1vet2t2upat2a of Turkey called the Janissary was
<>formed out of poor Christians captured in war, and that
<>of Egypt called Mamaluk was formed out of slaves.
<>But, the Ca1vet2t2upat2a of ancient Kerala was self-orga-
<>nised out of burning love for their king and country.
<>The families of those warriors of the pata who died in
<>fight were allotted royal favours. Even before, in the 14th
<>century A.D. there existed in Kerala this system of
<>Ca1vet2t2upat2a. From A.D. 1090 to 1111 A.D. many fierce
<>wars were fought between Kerala and the Cola country,
<>and it was perhaps during this period that this system of
<>fighting came into vogue. Certain inscriptions of the
<>period go to prove that Ra1mavarmakulas4ekhara Cakra-
<>varti who ruled Kerala during the above period drove
<>out the Colas from Quilon and captured places up to
<>Kot2t2ar.
<NI>Foreign writers have also referred to the Ca1vet2t2upat2a.
<>“Amouces” and “Amochi” used in the ‘Rise of Portu-
<>guese power in India’ indicate the Ca1vet2t2upat2a. “In
<>the war between Cochin and Calicut in 1504 three
<>princes of Cochin were killed, one of them being the
<>nephew of the ruling monarch. On his death 200
<>Ca1vet2t2u warriors who formed the body-guard of the
<>nephew rushed to the field after shaving their heads
<>and eyebrows and killed all the enemies they saw.”

<HI>CERIPPU. (FOOTWEAR). There is a story in
<>Maha1bha1rata of how Cerippu and Kut2a (footwear and
<>umbrella) were born. Once the heat of the Sun be-

<>the sage started sending arrows against the Sun. His

<>This continued without break and the Sun began to

<>under a banyan tree exhausted. When she became well

<>increased fury his shower of arrows and the Sun in the
<>disguise of a Brahmin approached and advised him that it
<>was not possible to strike down the Sun because he was
<>a swift-mover in the sky and so it was better to withdraw
<>from that attempt. But Jamadagni said the Sun would [Page182-a+ 65]
<>be stationary for some time at midday and then he would
<>hit the Sun down. When the Sun found that Jamadagni
<>would never drop his attempt he accepted defeat and
<>presented Jamadagni with a pair of sandals and an
<>umbrella to protect against the heat from below and
<>above. From that day onwards footwear and umbrella
<>came into vogue.
<NI>The practice of presenting sandals and umbrella is

<HI>DADHYAN3.
<F>1) The stories regarding the two hermits Dadhici and Dadhyan3 in the Pura1n2as are not very clear. In Maha1 bha1rata Dadhi1ca is men-
<>tioned as the son of Bhr2gu, and in R2gveda it occurs that Dadhi1ca was the son of Hermit Atharva who was the son of Vasis2t2ha.
<>Moreover the story of Dadhyan3 teaching the As4vini1devas the ‘Madhuvidya1’ is connected with Dadhici in some other pura1nas

<NI>After this, once the Pracetases (the ten sons of Barhis)

<>which Dhr2tara1s2t2ra's kingdom was the havis in the form
<>of sliced meat. This homa was performed in Avaki1rn2a-
<>maha1ti1rtha at Pr2thu1daka. As a result of it the kingdom

<HI>DAMANAKAM. The Ta1tiri tree (Grislea Tomentosa).
<>The ceremony of worshipping this tree is called Dama-
<>naka1rohan2avidhi. The Grislea tree is supposed to be
<>Bhairava, who had been changed to a tree by the curse
<>of S4iva. A story to this effect occurs in the Pura1n2as.
<NI>Bhairava was formed from the anger of S4iva. Bhairava,
<>against the will of S4iva, destroyed the devas, and so
<>S4iva cursed him and turned him to a Ta1tiri tree. It is
<>called Damanaka because Bhairava tried to do ‘damana’
<>(restraint or punishment) to the gods.
<NI>Bhairava felt sorry at the curse of S4iva. He requested
<>S4iva to withdraw the curse. At last S4iva had pity on him
<>and said that all would worship Damanaka tree. The
<>method of that worship is called Damanaka1rohan2a-
<>vidhi. It is given below:
<NI>This tree should be worshipped on the seventh or thir-
<>teenth lunar day. The worshipper should go to the
<>tree, with those who recite mantras and spells. After
<>the worship is over the worshipper should say, “O,
<>Tree, which has originated by the power of Hari, you
<>come to my presence. On behalf of S4iva, and by his
<>order, I have to take you home.” Saying thus the
<>tree should be taken home and consecrated in the even-
<>ing in accordance with the rituals. In the house, the
<>Sun, S4iva and Agni should be evoked and worshipped
<>and then the root of the tree should be planted in the
<>I1s4a1na (N.E. point) corner of the house and when it
<>is planted, the spell or incantation of Va1madeva Mantra
<>or S4iromantra should be recited. In the same way
<>the trunk with the branches of the tree is planted on
<>the Northern part. The fallen leaves and flowers
<>should be placed on the eastern side. When the root
<>is planted the following prayer should be uttered:
<Poem>A1mantritosi deves4a
<>pra1tah2 ka1le maya1 prabho /
<>Kartavyastapaso la1bha1h2
<>Pu1rn2am3 sarvam3 tava1jn5aya1. //</Poem>
<>After that at dawn he should take bath and with obla-
<>tions of sweet-smelling flowers etc. should worship
<>S4iva. This is Damanaka1rohan2avidhi. (Agni Pura1n2a,
<>Chapter 80).

<NI>5) {%Nala and Damayanti1 to the forest.%} Pus2kara got the

<HI>DAN2D2ANI1TI. (The laws of chastisement). Dan2d2a-
<>ni1ti is the law of punishment given to the subjects
<>by Kings of ancient India. According to the criminal
<>laws of ancient India, fining a man upto two hundred
<>and fifty pan2as (a coin) was called Prathama S4a1hasa
<>dan2d2a (first degree of punishment) and fining up to
<>five hundred pan2as was called Madhyama Sa1hasa [Page201-b+ 65]
<>dan2d2a (medium punishment) and fining upto thou-
<>sand pan2as was called Uttama Sa1hasa dan2d2a (highest
<>degree of punishment). If a man complains to
<>the King that his property is stolen, when actually
<>it is not stolen, the man will be fined the amount
<>that is said to have been stolen. There was another
<>law, that the owner of the stolen property and
<>the thief would have to pay double the amount
<>they admit, if the amount shown in the complaint
<>differed from the actual amount stolen. For appear-
<>ing as false witness, the three classes of non-Brahmins
<>were punished with fine and if he was a Brahmin he
<>would have to be cast out of the society. The King
<>ordered that if one spent the property entrusted with
<>him for keeping, the owner of the property would
<>have to be paid double the amount. If one says that
<>he has given the property for keeping when actually
<>it is not, the person will have to be punished as if he
<>were a thief. If a man spends an amount without
<>knowing that it was the property of others, the man
<>will have to be acquitted of the charge.
<NI>If an artisan has received money in advance for a parti-
<>cular product and fails to give the thing at the stipu-
<>lated time the King will fine the artisan one svarn2a.
<>If a man received money in advance on a promise to
<>do a particular work and if he fails to do the work he
<>will be fined one Kr2s2n2ala of gold. (One Kr2s2n2ala
<>weighs three yavagrains). If a man conceals his diseases
<>and marries a damsel, she will be considered as a spins-
<>ter and the man will be fined two hundred pan2as.
<>If a cowherd agrees to look after the cows of another
<>receiving pay and food and refuses to return the cow
<>to the owner the King will fine him hundred pan2as.
<>If a Ks2atriya scoffed a Bra1hman2a the fine imposed
<>would be hundred pan2as. If it is a Vais4ya the fine will
<>be two hundred pan2as. If it is a S4u1dra he will be put
<>to death. If a Brahmin scoffs a Ks2atriya the fine is
<>fifty pan2as. If a S4u1dra scoffs a Vais4ya the fine is twenty-
<>five pan2as. If a Brahmin scoffs a S4u1dra the fine is
<>only twelve pan2as. If a S4u1dra scoffs a Ks2atriya his
<>tongue should be cut off. If a S4u1dra advises a Brahmin,
<>he may inflict any punishment on the S4u1dra.
<NI>If a S4u1dra wronged a Brahmin, the S4u1dra might be
<>punished by cutting off the organ which was employed
<>in the crime. If one spat at a Brahmin, the two lips of
<>the culprit might be cut off. If a man passed urine on a
<>Brahmin the culprit would have his penis cut off. If
<>a S4u1dra sits on the seats of the upper classes his but-
<>tock will have to be cut off. If one slays cow, elephant,
<>camel or horse half of his limbs will have to be cut
<>off. Cutting across a road, changing of boundaries,
<>making the water of pools and ponds impure etc. will
<>have to be punished with a fine of two suvarn2as. (Agni
<>Pura1n2a, Chapter 227).

<NI>10) {%The boon of S4ani (Saturn).%} Astronomers are of
<>opinion that famine will occur in the world for the

<NI>During the regime of Das4aratha the planet S4ani approa-
<>ched the orbit of Rohin2i1. Experts in astronomy said that
<>the earth would be ruined by famine etc. if S4ani cleft

<>and arrows, got into his chariot, and started for the

<>yojanas (leagues) and reached the hind part of Rohin2i1,
<>which is beyond the sun. Adorned with golden gar-

<>on a golden chariot decorated with precious stones, and a
<>lofty flagpost and yoked with horses of the colour of
<>swan, the king shone in the sky as a second sun. He drew
<>the bow-string right upto his ear and placed in it the

<>saw the arrow of destruction they began to tremble with
<>fear. S4ani came to Das4aratha and fell before him and

<>ratha told S4ani that he only wanted S4ani not to come to

<>S4ani has never entered the orbit of Rohin2i1. (Padma

<HI>DASYU. The ancient dwellers of North India. What
<>we see in R2gveda is mostly a history of the A1ryans from
<>the period of their exodus from the plateau Kumbha
<>till they reached the banks of the Yamuna1. The plateau
<>of Kum3bha is Kabul. The Dasyus were the first people
<>the Aryans had to confront with after passing the Indus.
<>R2gveda bears testimony to the fact that the civilization
<>of the Dasyus was far advanced than that of the A1ryans.
<>S4am3bara, King of the Dasyus, was the ruler of hundred
<>cities. All the cities were fortified with strong walls and
<>fortresses, which are described as ‘as4vamayi1’, ‘a1yasi1’,
<>‘s4atabhuji1’ etc. The greatest enemies of the A1ryans were
<>the ‘Pan2is’ of these cities. They were a particular class
<>of people of these cities. In the ‘Nirukta of Ya1ska’ it is
<>mentioned that pan2is were traders. Names of many of the
<>Kings of the Dasyus occur in the R2gveda. Dhuni,
<>Cumuri, Pipru, Varcas, S4am3bara and such others are the
<>most valiant and mighty among them. The most impor-
<>tant of the several tribes of the Dasyus were the S4imyus,
<>the Ki1kat2as, S4igrus and the Yaks2us. They are mentioned
<>as the Ana1sas in the R2gveda. (Ana1sas--without nose).
<>Perhaps their nose was flat; more over they are stated as
<>having dark complexion. So it may be assumed that the
<>Dasyus were Dravidians. They talked a primitive
<>language, and they despised sacrificial religion. They did
<>not worship Gods like Indra and others. They possibly
<>worshipped the Phallus, S4iva, Devi and the like.

<HI>DA1YAKRAMA. (INHERITANCE). Da1yakrama is [Page207-a+ 63]
<>the system by which the wealth of parents is received by
<>the heirs. The system of inheritance as described by Manu
<>is as follows:--
<NI>1) After the death of the parents, all the children should
<>divide their wealth among themselves. When either the
<>father or the mother is alive, the sons should not take
<>their wealth.
<NI>2) If the wealth is not divided, the eldest brother should
<>keep the whole of it in his custody and maintain his
<>brothers and sisters like a father.
<NI>3) Of the entire wealth, the eldest brother may take one-
<>twentieth part, the second brother, one-fortieth part
<>and the third brother, one-eghtieth part and the balance
<>is to be divided equally among all of them.
<NI>4) If there are more than three sons, the eldest and the
<>youngest may take one-twentieth and one-eightieth (of
<>the entire wealth) respectively, and each of the other
<>brothers may take one-fortieth. The rest of the pro-
<>perty must be divided equally among all of them.
<NI>5) After dividing like this, if there are unmarried sisters,
<>each of the brothers should give one-fourth of his share
<>for their marriage.
<NI>6) The ornaments which the mother had received by
<>way of her dowry etc. may be taken after her death by
<>her unmarried daughters.
<NI>7) If, after his marriage, one of the brothers dies, the
<>brother who keeps his movable and immovable proper-
<>ties, must beget children by the brother's wife and hand
<>over the above properties to her issue. (See under
<>Manusmr2ti).

<HI>DEVA(S). Gods or deities.
<NI>1) {%General information.%} From time immemorial belief in
<>Devas has existed in every country and all religions have
<>lauded their superior nature and power. It was the
<>Hindus and the Buddhists who first applied the term ‘Deva’
<>to certain very subtle beings recognised in all religions.
<>The Pa1rsi religion (Zaratus2t2ra) has spoken about seven
<>Devara1jans and their attendants. ‘Ames2 pentas’ is the
<>actual term used for the Devara1ja. The Christian reli-
<>gion refers to nine sects of Devas like Sra1fi, Kherubi,
<>Dominion, Angel etc. I1slam refers to four chief Devas
<>viz. Gabriel, the presiding Deva over revelations, Mik-
<>hayel of protection, Asriyal of death and Israfin of resur-
<>ruction. An important section of the R2gveda is Su1ktas
<>about Deva1s like Indra, Mitra, Varun2a, Agni etc. In
<>Yajn5as etc. Devas occupy a very important place. The
<>Kenopanis2ad states that the conceited and haughty Devas
<>were taught a lesson by God. The subject matter of the
<>Kat2hopanis2ad is the advice given by Yama to Naciketas.
<>The Mun2d2akopanis2ad says that the Devas, man and
<>birds originated from God.
<F>1. Tasma1cca deva1h2 bahudha1 samprasu1ta1h2 sa1dhya1h2 manus2ya1h2 pas4avo vaya1m3sah2.</F> There are references about
<>Deva worship in the Smr2tis. The Pura1n2as and Upapu- [Page207-b+ 62]
<>ra1n2as contain scientific discussions, about the origin,
<>work or functions, classes, etc. of Devas. The Mantra-
<>s4a1stra and Tantras4a1stra deal also about the various sects
<>and class of Devas, their nature, and the worship to be
<>offered to them etc.
<NI>2) {%Christian Devas, Satan and devils.%} Christian religious
<>books commonly use the term Ma1la1khas for Devas.
<>Greek mythology contains a story about the Ma1la1khas,
<>who did not obey the orders of Jehovah and how He
<>cursed them, turned them into devils and flung them into
<>hell. And, in hell they organised a revolutionary party
<>to fight Jehovah. Many leaders talked on the subject of
<>how to take vengeance on Jehovah. It was nearabout
<>this period that Jehovah created with the dust on earth
<>Adam as his beloved son and settled him in the garden of
<>Aden. God created from the ribs of Adam the woman
<>called Eve, and they lived in Eden quite happily.
<NI>Satan and other leaders in hell decided that the greatest
<>revenge that could be taken upon Jehovah was to create
<>troubles for his dear son, Adam in Eden. Accordingly
<>Satan went to Eden and made Adam and Eve eat the
<>forbidden fruit with the result that Jehovah cursed and
<>turned them into human beings and turned them out of
<>Eden. Milton in his reputed poem Paradise Lost has told
<>the above story in inimitable language.
<NI>3) {%Indian Devas.%} Most of the Indian Devas are the sons
<>of Kas4yapa Praja1pati by Aditi, daughter of Daks2a Praja1-
<>pati. The total number of Devas is 33 crores. The Devas
<>are divided into many classes or sections like A1dityas,
<>Vis4vadevatas, Vasus, Tus2itas, A1bha1svaras, Anilas, Maha1-
<>ra1jikas, Sa1dhyas, Rudras, Vidya1dharas, Pitr2devas etc.

<>etc. Yet another division is into Lokapa1las, Lipikas etc.
<>The Devas are classified with special reference to
<>bhu1tagan2as like Pr2thvi1 etc. and are, therefore, referred
<>to as Bhu1devata1s, Agnidevata1s, Va1yudevata1s, etc. The
<>presiding spirit of Bhu1devata1s is Kubera, that of the
<>Jaladevata1s is Varun2a, that of the Agnidevata1s, Va1yu-
<>bhagava1n and that of the A1ka1s4adevatas, Indra. And,
<>under them there are various sets of Devas in charge of
<>different departments. Sa1dhyas, Vasus, A1dityas, Apsaras

<HI>DEVADATTA I. A famous brahmin boy whose story is
<>described in the Katha1saritsa1gara.
<NI>Devadatta was the son of the Brahmin, Haridatta of
<>Kambukapura. Though as a boy Devadatta learnt all
<>the arts and sciences when he grew up to be a youth he
<>became a very wayward fellow. Dice-play became his

<>clothes, and being afraid of his father, he left the place
<>without returning home.
<NI>Devadatta roamed about, and during one such trip
<>he saw a deserted temple, and a muni called Ja1lapa1da
<>engaged in reciting mantras. Devadatta prostrated be-
<>fore the muni and told him all the details about himself.
<>The muni accepted Devadatta as his s4is2ya and promised
<>to secure vidya1dharahood for him.
<NI>Next night Ja1lapa1da led Devadatta to a burning ghat, [Page208-b+ 64]
<>nearby the temple. After conducting Pu1ja1 in the shade
<>of a fig tree with offerings of Pa1yasa and Vais4va-
<>devabali the muni told Devadatta thus: “You should
<>come here daily and perform pu1ja1 like this, and pray
<>at the close of it, ‘Oh! Vidyutprabha1! please accept my
<>pu1ja1.’
<NI>Devadatta acted according to the above advice of the
<>muni, and one day, at the close of his pu1ja1 the tree broke
<>open into two and a beautiful female who appeared from
<>it took him with her saying that her mistress wanted him.
<>He was thus taken to a house studded with gems wherein
<>he saw a noble lady seated on a cot. She caught Deva-
<>datta by his hands and after seating him alongside said

<>king Ratnavars2a. I am a virgin girl. Muni Ja1lapa1da
<>has worshipped me so much that I have decided to
<>fulfil his desire. I am in love with you and you will
<>please wed me.”
<NI>Accordingly Devadatta married Vidyutprabha1 and lived
<>there with her. In due course she conceived, and Deva-
<>datta met Ja1lapa1da and told him about the whole
<>affair, and the muni, to achieve his personal object
<>asked Devadatta to cut open the abdomen of Vidyut-
<>prabha1 and take to him the child found therein. Deva-
<>datta did not at all relish the idea. Yet reluctant to
<>disobey his preceptor he returned to his wife. She permit-
<>ted him to carry out the directions of the muni, yet his
<>mind did not approve of the action. Then Vidyutprabha1
<>herself cut open her abdomen, took the child out of it

<>“He who eats the child will become a Vidya1dhara.
<>Take it. I was a Vidya1dhari1 turned into a Yaks2i1 by a
<>curse, and to cut open my abdomen and take out the
<>child like this was the redemption promised me from the
<>curse, and now I go to the Vidya1dhara world; we shall
<>meet there.” And she disappeared.
<NI>In great sorrow Devadatta brought the child to Ja1la-
<>pa1da who, after sending him out on the pretext of his
<>(Ja1lapa1da's) performing Bhairavapu1ja, ate up the child.

<>Devadatta made up his mind to anyhow take revenge

<>the help of a Veta1la whom he befriended by offering
<>human flesh. And, there he saw Ja1lapa1da drunk with
<>pride at his Vidya1dharahood sitting on a throne of
<>gems in a mansion. Meanwhile Vidyutprabha1 who was
<>now once more a Vidya1dhari1 had turned down the
<>advances made by the erstwhile Ja1lapa1da for her love.
<>But, at the sight of Devadatta her face flushed with love

<NI>Devapratima1s (idols) are of seven varieties like those
<>made of earth, of wood, of metals, of gems, of sandal
<>wood, of stone and of flowers. Of the above, idols made
<>of earth, sandalwood and of flowers are meant only for
<>temporary use, but they also grant all the desires of the
<>devotees.
<NI>Stone for idols should be got from mountains. Pa1n2d2ura
<>(white), Arun2a (red), Pi1ta (yellow) and Kr2s2n2a (black)-
<>rocks having any one of these four colours may be
<>selected. If no such stone is available any other stone
<>may be used, but by doing homa and reciting Narasim3ha
<>mantra the attributes of any of the specified varn2as
<>should be transferred to it. It is best to have white
<>markings on the stone selected for the idol. There are
<>the three genders, masculine, feminine and neuter with
<>reference to stones. Stone which produces the sound of
<>bell metal on being hit and gives out sparks of fire on
<>being cut is of the masculine gender. Stone which
<>possesses these attributes to a lesser degree is of the
<>feminine gender. Stone with no shape is of neuter gen-
<>der. Beside these three varieties there are the sagarbha
<>(pregnant) stones also, viz. stones with round markings
<>on them, and they should not be used for making idols.
<>Once it is decided to make an idol, Vanayajn5a should
<>be performed first. To worship the forest from which
<>the stone for the idol was to be obtained is vanayajn5a.
<>A specified place in the forest should be dug up, the
<>pit treated with cow-dung and a small platform raised
<>and Vis2n2u worshipped thereon. After sacrificial offerings
<>etc. instruments for the construction of the idol like
<>t2an3ka (chisel) should be worshipped. To sprinkle on
<>the stone s4a1litoya (water in which paddy grains are
<>put) purified with the chanting of astramantra is the
<>next step. After that bhu1tabali (offerings to the spirits
<>of the stone) should be performed upon which the
<>bhu1tas residing inside the stone will quit. Then the
<>a1ca1rya should go to sleep repeating the svapna mantra.

<HI>DEVAS4ARMA1 II. A Brahmin, an erudite scholar in the

<NI>Devas4arman, the very erudite brahmin scholar in the

<NI>{%Dog :%}--Please attend to my words about what my

<NI>“Look here, the ox was, in its previous birth, a great
