<HI>VAIS4VADEVA(M). A sacrifice. It is mentioned in
<>Devi1 Bha1gavata, Skandha 11, that a brahmin should
<>perform this sacrifice to protect himself from hurts
<>caused by oven, threshing stone, axe, cutting knife, and
<>other weapons. This sacrifice could be performed in a
<>cavity for kindling fire on the floor besmeared with
<>cowdung and mud. It should not be done in an
<>ordinary oven meant for cooking, in iron oven, in
<>earthernware or on ordinary floor. As all the deities
<>are having faces of fire, the sacrificial fire should not be
<>kindled by fanning the flame with hand, winnow, hide
<>of black antelope or cloth. By fanning the flame with
<>cloth, the sacrificer will contract disease; by winnowing
<>he would sustain loss of wealth; and death, by fanning
<>with hand. Plums, fruits, roots, curd, ghee etc. could
<>be used as burnt offerings. When these are not avail-
<>able, firewood, roots of herbs, grass etc. could be used
<>instead. Things to be offered as burnt-offerings should
<>be purified, first by sprinkling ghee on them. In the
<>absence of ghee, milk, curd and water may be used.
<>Using things which are unfit as burnt-offerings will
<>invite bad results.
<NI>In Vais4vadeva-sacrifice, half-burnt firewood used in
<>cooking, should never be used. So also salts of any
<>kind. After finishing Vais4vadeva, Gogra1sa (giving rice
<>to cow) also should be done.

<HI>VAJRA1YUDHA (Thunderbolt). The famous weapon
<>of Indra.
<NI>1) {%The making of this weapon.%} In olden days a fierce
<>asura named Vr2tra was born. The Ka1lakeyas and
<>many other asuras became his followers. They began to
<>create havoc in the world, and cause harm to the
<>Devas. At last under the leadership of Indra, the Devas
<>went to Brahma1 and informed him of their grievances
<>and requested for advice as to the way of killing Vr2tra.
<>Brahma1 told them that only with a weapon made of the
<>bone of the hermit Dadhi1ca, could Vr2tra1sura be killed.
<>The Devas went to the bank of the river S4on2a and saw
<>the hermit Dadhi1ca, who was the foremost of munificent
<>men, doing penance there. Indra told him the purpose
<>of their visit. He told the Devas to take his bone, if it
<>was useful to them. Saying this he forsook his body. The
<>Devas took the bones of the hermit and gave them to
<>Vis4vakarma1 who made a powerful weapon with them
<>and gave that to Indra. They named the weapon the
<>‘thunderbolt.’ (M.B. Vana Parva, Chapter 100).
<NI>2) {%The face of Subrahman2ya was cut.%} Once Indra was
<>defeated by Naraka1sura. He went to the Hima1layas and
<>hid himself there. Unable to see their King Indra, the
<>devas went to Subrahman2ya. When Indra knew this, he
<>thought that Subrahman2ya had taken possession of the
<>world of the gods. So he came and fought with Su-
<>brahman2ya. The thunderbolt of Indra touched the face
<>of Subrahman2ya and wounded him. From the blood
<>which flowed from the face of Subrahman2ya two noble
<>men appeared who eventually became warriors of
<>Subrahman2ya. (Katha1saritsa1gara, La1va1n2akalambaka,
<>Taran3ga 6). [Page822-a+ 64]
<NI>3) {%Daily thunderbolt.%} In Vis2n2u Pura1n2a, Am3s4a 1, Chap-
<>ter 5 and Am3s4a 2, Chapter 8, a process by which
<>thunderbolt is made daily in the evening from the water
<>particles thrown by Brahmins when they recite the spell
<>Ga1yatri1, is described.
<NI>In the evening, the fierce giants called the Mandehas
<>wish to eat the Sun. Praja1pati had given them a curse
<>that though their bodies would not perish they would
<>daily meet with death. So there is a fight between these
<>giants and the sun daily in the evening. At that time
<>the Brahmins recite the spell Ga1yatri1 with the Brahma-
<>pervading syllable ‘OM,’ and throw up water. This
<>water becomes the Vajra weapon, and burns the giant.
<NI>4) {%The thunderbolt became a tiger.%} The hermits Na1rada
<>and Parvata once went to the palace of the King
<>Sr2n5jaya. The King worshipped them and served
<>them for a long time, as a result of which a son was
<>born to him. Indra decided to lessen the superior
<>power of these hermits. Once the son of the King, who
<>was a mere boy, was playing in the forest. At the in-
<>struction of Indra, the thunderbold took the form of a
<>tiger and went to the forest and killed the boy. Sr2n5jaya
<>became very sad. Na1rada and Parvata brought the boy
<>to lite again and gave him to the King. (M.B. S4a1nti
<>Parva, Chapter 30).

<HI>VA1KPA1RUS2YA (Using harsh words). One of the
<>wrongs brought under the rule of chastisement in ancient
<>India. Without caring for the truth or falsity, a man
<>praising another with a view to tease or offend him,
<>is Va1kpa1rusya. The teasing may be aimed at some-
<>body with disabled members of the body or disabled
<>organs of sense. Besides, using heart-rending words also [Page822-b+ 65]
<>comes under this crime. In olden days kings issued
<>orders to fine anybody found guilty of this crime. Ordi-
<>narily the fine was 25 Pan2as. If the crime was committ-
<>ed against one who was below the level of the culprit
<>the fine to be paid was only half. If harsh words were
<>used against other women or people of a higher level
<>the fine was double. (Agni Pura1n2a, Chapter 258).

<HI>VA1LMI1KI I. A hermit who was the first among poets
<>and the author of Ra1ma1yan2a.
<NI>1) {%General information.%} Knowledge about this hermit
<>who was the first among the poets of Bha1rata, is scanty.
<>So we have to depend mainly on some hearsay for the
<>life history of this sage.
<NI>It is said that Va1lmi1ki was the tenth son of Varun2a. But
<>in his younger age he fell into the hands of wicked
<>people and became a wicked man, like his friends. Then
<>his name was not Va1lmi1ki. Being a father, he had to
<>support his family. For this purpose he used to plunder
<>travellers. Once he happened to catch the Saptars2is
<>(the seven hermits) who passed by that way. The
<>hermits asked him whether his wife and children would
<>share the sins he had incurred by plundering. The
<>plunderer could not answer that unexpected question.
<>He ran home and asked his wife and children if they
<>would share the sins incurred by him. They were not
<>prepared to do so. In a moment his life underwent a
<>thorough change. He ran to the Saptars2is and knelt
<>before them. They imparted to the forester, knowledge
<>of the Vedas. The forester sat under a tree and began
<>to sing ‘Ra1ma Ra1ma.’ Days and months and years
<>passed, unknown to him. He did not know that white
<>ants had built a shelter above him. After several years
<>the Saptars2is returned by that way. They broke the [Page823-a+ 65]
<>ant-hill and took the hermit out. Because he came out
<>of Valmi1ka or white-ant-hill he came to be known as
<>Va1lmi1ki. He built his hermitage on the bank of the
<>river Tamasa1 and lived there with his disciples. It was
<>at this place that he composed the famous poem Ra1ma1-
<>yan2a. (For further details see under Ra1ma1yan2a).
<NI>2) {%Other details.%}
<NI>(1) Va1lmi1ki shines in the palace of Indra. (M.B.
<>Sabha1 Parva, Chapter 7, Stanza 16).
<NI>(ii) Mention is made in Maha1bha1rata, Udyoga Parva,
<>Chapter 83, Stanza 27, that Va1lmi1ki met S4ri1 Kr2s2n2a
<>who was going to Hastina1pura as a messenger of the
<>Pa1n2d2avas.
<NI>(iii) Sa1tyaki recited a poem composed by Va1lmi1ki,
<>after having killed Bhu1ris4ravas in the Bha1rata-battle.
<>(M.B. Dron2a Parva, Chapter 143, Stanza 57).
<NI>(iv) Va1lmi1ki told Yudhis2t2hira of the benefits of his
<>devotion to S4iva. (M.B. Anus4a1sana Parva, Chapter
<>18, Stanza 8).
<HI>VA1LMI1KI II. One of the prominent sons of Garud2a.

<HI>VA1MADEVA. An ancient hermit.
<NI>1) {%Va1madeva and S4ala.%} Three sons named S4ala, Dala
<>and Bala were born to King Pari1ks2it by his wife Sus4o-
<>bhana1, a princess of Man2d2u1ka. In due course, King
<>Pari1ks2it anointed his eldest son S4ala as King and went
<>to the forest for penance.
<NI>Once S4ala went to the forest to hunt. While chasing
<>a deer, the King asked his charioteer to bring horses
<>capable of overtaking the deer. The charioteer told the
<>King that such horses were available at the hermitage
<>of Va1madeva. They went to the hermitage of Va1ma-
<>deva and got the horses on condition that they would
<>be returned.
<NI>After the hunting, S4ala reached his capital. Seeing the
<>beauty and the vigorous nature of the horses, the King
<>did not like to part with them. Va1madeva sent his
<>disciple to the court of the King to take the horses back.
<>But the King sent him back empty-handed. Va1madeva
<>got angry. He came in person and demanded his horses.
<>The King replied that Brahmins did not require such
<>horses. While these two were quarrelling with each
<>other, some fierce giants came there and pierced S4ala
<>with a trident and killed him. (M.B. Vana Parva,
<>Chapter 192).
<NI>2) {%Other information.%}
<NI>(i) He was a friend of Vasis2t2ha and a priest of Das4aratha.
<>(Va1lmi1ki Ra1ma1yan2a, Ba1laka1n2d2a. Sarga 7, Stanza 3).
<NI>(ii) Man2d2ala 4 of R2gveda was composed by Va1madeva.
<NI>(iii) Va1madeva was a hermit who had praised the
<>As4vini1devas when he was in his mother's womb.
<>(R2gveda, Man2d2ala 1, Su1kta 119).
<NI>(iv) Once Va1madeva tried to eat the flesh of a dog
<>because of hunger, with a view to save Brahmins.
<>(Manusmr2ti, Chapter 10, Stanza 106).
<NI>(v) He was a prominent member in the assembly of
<>Indra. (M.B. Sabha1 Parva, Chapter 7, Stanza 17).
<NI>(vi) Once Va1madeva gave advice about righteousness
<>to King Vasumanas. (M.B. S4a1nti Parva, Chapter 92).
<HI>VA1MADEVA II. A King. Arjuna defeated this King

<HI>VA1MANA I. An incarnation of Maha1vis2n2u.
<NI>1) {%General information.%} There are ten main incarnations
<>of Maha1vis2n2u. Of these, the incarnation of Va1mana is
<>the fifth.
<NI>2) {%Two Va1manas.%} Two different stories occur in the
<>Pura1n2as about the incarnation of Va1mana. One story
<>is about how Maha1vis2n2u took the incarnation of Va1mana
<>and thrust Maha1bali an asura, down to the nether-
<>world. This story is more widely known. In the second
<>story the place of Maha1bali is given to the asura called
<>Dhundhu. This is the main difference. For a compara-
<>tive study, both stories are given below:
<NI>a) {%The first story of the incarnation of Va1mana.%} The devas
<>(gods) such as Indra and the others were born to Praja1-
<>pati Kas4yapa by his wife Aditi and the asuras (demons)
<>such as Maha1bali and others, by his wife Diti. The
<>Daityas (asuras) began to harm and harass the Devas
<>to a great extent. Once Aditi, the mother of the Devas,
<>complained to Kas4yapa about this. He advised her to
<>take the fast called ‘Payovrata’ fixing the image of
<>Maha1vis2n2u in her heart and that he will take birth
<>through her as Va1mana and destroy Maha1bali. Accord-
<>ing to the advice of her husband, Aditi began to take
<>Payovrata, at the end of which Maha1vis2n2u appeared
<>before her and asked her what her wish was. She told
<>Vis2n2u, of her grievances and Vis2n2u consoled her and
<>said “You have invoked me by your prayer and fast
<>for the safety of your sons. So I will enter your womb
<>through the penance of Kas4yapa and take birth as your
<>son and rescue your sons.”
<NI>Maha1vis2n2u disappeared. Aditi worshipped her husband
<>with devotion. By contemplation Kas4yapa knew every-
<>thing. He infused the energy he had acquired by
<>penance into Aditi, who gave birth to a son. The birth
<>took place on the twelfth day of the month of Bha1dra-
<>pada, in the bright lunar fortnight at the auspicious
<>moment called Abhijit, in the star of S4ra1van2a. The
<>infant had four hands. While Kas4yapa and Aditi were
<>looking on, the infant changed its form and became a
<>dwarfish Brahmin boy. The Devas brought presents
<>to the child. The Sun taught him the spell called Sa1vitri1-
<>mantra. Br2haspati gave the Brahmastring. Kas4yapa
<>gave the string worn round the waist. The earth gave
<>the hide of a black antelope. Soma the Vanaspati gave
<>a rod; Aditi gave the cloth over the privities, the sky
<>an umbrella, the seven hermits gave Kus4a-grass, Brahma1
<>gave a waterpot, Sarasvati1 gave a rosary and Kubera
<>gave a pot.
<NI>At that time, the powerful Maha1bali had brought the
<>three worlds of heaven, earth and Pa1ta1la (the nether-
<>world) under his control. That Asura King performed
<>a horse-sacrifice with the help of a Bha1rgava Brahmin.
<>Hearing about it Va1mana started for the place of sacri-
<>fice. Maha1bali was performing the sacrifice at a place
<>called Bhr2gukacchaka on the North bank of river
<>Narmada1. The priests who were performing the rites [Page824-a+ 65]
<>and ceremonies of the sacrifice saw Va1mana coming
<>slowly to the sacrificial hall. They wondered whether it
<>was the Sun, Sanatkuma1ra or Agni (Fire) coming to
<>see the sacrifice. While they were standing thus, Va1mana
<>with his umbrella, rod and water pot filled with water
<>entered the sacrificial hall. Maha1bali welcomed Va1mana
<>and asked him the purpose of his visit. Va1mana said
<>“Oh King! Your words are sweet. Noble Asura! give
<>me three feet of ground which I measure with my feet.
<>That is all what I want.”
<NI>Maha1bali agreed. The teacher-priest S4ukra felt some
<>doubts regarding the identity of Va1mana. So he secret-
<>ly told Maha1bali that the boy Va1mana was none other
<>than Maha1vis2n2u and as such, he should not give any
<>promise. But Maha1bali had already given the promise.
<>He refused to go back upon his words. The priest
<>S4ukra got angry at this and cursed Maha1bali thus.
<>“You boast that you are wise and learned. But you are
<>disobedient, slow-witted and unwise. So all your
<>prosperities will be destroyed.”
<NI>Though he was cursed, he did not deviate from the
<>path of truth. He gave the promised ground to
<>Va1mana by pouring water with the water brought
<>in golden pot by his queen Vindhya1vali1. The names,
<>As4ana1 and Kot2ara1 also are used in the Pura1n2as for
<>Vindhya1vali1 the wife of Maha1bali. She came out for
<>the purpose wearing golden ornaments. Maha1bali
<>himself washed the feet of Va1mana, who instantly
<>began to grow and became large beyond imagination.
<>Everybody on the spot was amazed at the unimagin-
<>able bigness of Va1mana. On that huge figure, Maha1bali
<>saw the priest, the performers of sacrificial rites, the sacri-
<>ficial hall, the universe, the elements, the qualities the
<>senses, the mind, the individual spirits, and at the feet
<>of the figure the world Rasa1tala. He saw the earth on
<>its feet, mountains below the knees, birds on its knees,
<>the Maruts on its thighs, evening on its clothes, the
<>Praja1patis on its privities, the noble and mighty asuras
<>on its lions, the sky on its navel, the oceans on its stomach,
<>Dharma (duty) in its heart, rightness and truth on its
<>breasts, Maha1laks2mi1 holding lotus on its chest, songs
<>of Sa1man and all other voices in its neck, all the gods
<>beginning with Indra on its hands, the points (direct-
<>ions) on its ears, the ether on its head, the clouds on
<>its hair, breaths in its nose, the sun in its eyes, fire on
<>its face, the Vedas in its words, Varun2a in its tongue,
<>day and night agreement and disagreement in its wink-
<>ing and anger on its forehead. In its touch there was
<>desire, in its radiance there was water, in its buttocks
<>Jawlessness, sacrifice in its steps, death in its shadow,
<>illusion in its laugh, medicines in its hairs, rivers in its
<>veins, stones in its nails, Brahma1 in its intelligence,
<>hermits, devas etc. in its life-breaths. Thus the figure
<>was seen by Maha1bali. Va1mana had trodden on the
<>whole of the earth, which was completely under the
<>cont ol of Maha1bali, with one foot, filled the whole of
<>the sky with his large body and the four points were filled
<>with his hands. The second step was put on Maharloka,
<>Janaloka and Tapoloka (three worlds). No spot was
<>left in the universe for a third step.
<NI>Va1mana said:--“You have given me three feet of
<>ground. I have measured two feet of ground. Show me
<>the place to measure the third step. I have measured
<>the earth with one step and the heaven with the second
<>step. You have seen it. If you cannot keep your promise [Page824-b+ 65]
<>you had better go down to Pa1ta1la.” Bali requested him
<>to place the third step on his head. Va1mana placed his
<>foot on the head of Maha1bali and thrust him down to
<>Pa1ta1la.
<NI>Va1mana brought Indra to the spot and anointed him
<>as the ruler of heaven, in the presence of all the gods
<>and hermits. Indra sent Va1mana with the Lokapa1las
<>(Indra, Agni, Yama and Varun2a) in a divine Vima1na
<>to the world of Vis2n2u. (Bha1gavata Skandha 8).
<NI>b) {%The second story of the incarnation of Va1mana.%} Dhundhu,
<>an asura boy, was born to Kas4yapa by his wife Danu.
<>That asura did penance and pleased Brahma1. He made
<>a request that he should not be killed by Indra and
<>the other gods or anybody else. Brahma1, who was
<>pleased at his penance, gave him the boon he asked.
<>The boy Dhundhu, at the beginning of the fourth
<>Kaliyuga, during the period of Hiran2yakas4ipu, went to
<>heaven and defeating Indra and the other Devas,
<>established his rule there as Indra. The mighty
<>Hiran2yakas4ipu was travelling on the mountain Mandara
<>as an official under Dhundhu.
<NI>The defeated and grief-stricken Devas went to the
<>world of Brahma1 and lived there. Dhundhu, who knew
<>this, wanted to drive them out of that place also. He
<>requested S4ukra, the priest and teacher of asuras, to
<>tell him the means of doing it.
<NI>S4ukra said. “Devendra was enabled to enter the
<>presence of Brahma1, because he had performed one
<>hundred horse-sacrifices. “Hearing this, Dhundhu, with
<>the permission of the teacher S4ukra, began to perform
<>sacrifice in the holy place called Pra1ci1na ti1rtha.
<NI>Hearing that Dhundhu had begun the horse-sacrifice,
<>Indra and the Devas trembled with fear and, leaving
<>the world of Brahma1, went to the world of Vis2n2u and
<>prayed for protection. Bhagava1n came to know of
<>everything and consoled them and sent them back.
<>After this Maha1vis2n2u took the form of a Va1mana
<>and jumped into the Devika1jala and lay afloat like a
<>piece of dry wood. Dhundhu and the hermits saw by
<>chance, Va1mana sinking and coming up in the water.
<>They took the Va1mana-Brahmin out of water and asked
<>him how he had fallen in water. Va1mana replied with
<>shiver:--“In the family of Varun2a there was a Brahmin
<>named Prabha1sa, who was a scholar. I am Gatibha1sa,
<>the younger of his two sons. After the death of father,
<>I requested my brother to divide the property of our
<>father. My brother quoted several rules and said that
<>I was not entitled to get any portion of my father's
<>wealth. I spoke against him and getting angry he
<>caught me by my hair and threw me into the river. It
<>is a year since I, being not able to swim, began to sink
<>and come up in this river. Thus you have seen me
<>here.”
<NI>The Bha1rgavas who were present there, requested
<>Dhundhu thus. “Oh! King of the asuras! Be pleased
<>to give this boy a well-furnished house, servant-maids
<>and plenty of wealth.” Hearing this Dhundhu said to
<>Va1mana. “I will provide you with wealth, servant-
<>maids, house, gold, cows, land, clothes etc.”
<NI>Va1mana humbly said to Dhundhu “Oh Lord! I do
<>not want any wealth. It is my desire for wealth that
<>has brought me to this plight. I request you to give
<>me only three feet of ground.”
<NI>As soon as the asura-King complied with his request,
<>Va1mana began to grow like the moon. He assumed the [Page825-a+ 62]
<>shape of Trivikrama to measure each of the three
<>worlds with a foot. In two steps he measured all the
<>worlds. Va1mana whose body was bigger than Maha1-
<>meru became angry when he did not see place to
<>measure the third step, and fell on Dhundhu. By this
<>heavy fall there appeared a great cavity thirty thousand
<>yojanas deep. Bhagava1n Vis2n2u took the asura Dhundhu
<>and threw him into that deep pit with a mighty force,
<>and by a shower of dust he filled the cavity.
<NI>Indra with the Devas occupied the world of Gods.
<>Leaving the asura King in the sea of dust, Bhagava1n
<>jumped into the river Ka1lindi1 and disappeared. (Padma
<>Pura1n2a, Chapter 78).

<NI>The social life of the monkeys, is described as follows
<>in the Va1lmi1ki Ra1ma1yan2a, Kis2kindha1 Ka1n2d2a, Sarga
<>33. “Mahendra mountain, the Hima1layas, the Vindhya
<>mountain, the peaks of Kaila1sa and S4veta mountain,
<>Mandara mountain etc. are the places mostly inhabit-
<>ed by monkeys. On the mountains shining like the
<>rising sun, on the east of the western ocean also monkeys

<HI>VARA1HA III. (Boar). One of the ten incarnations of

<NI>1) {%Need for this incarnation.%} Jaya and Vijaya, two door-

<NI>Even their birth itself was inauspicious. Once, while

<NI>The elder son was called Hiran2ya1ks2a and the second
<>son was called Hiran2yakas4ipu. As Hiran2ya1ks2a grew up

<>The Devas went to Maha1vis2n2u and prayed to him in
<>order to get the earth back.
<NI>At this time Manu Sva1yambhuva, the son of Brahma1,

<>bhuva worshipped Devi1 with ardent devotion, deep
<>meditation and severe vows and penance, at which
<>Jagadamba1 was pleased. She appeared before him and
<>asked him what boon he wanted. Manu requested that
<>he should be permitted to carry on creation without
<>any obstruction. Devi1 gave him permission. Manu [Page827-a+ 65]
<>returned to his father Brahma1 and said. “Father, point
<>out to me a solitary place. I will sit there and create
<>subjects by the blessings of Devi1.” Only when he heard

<>the exigency of providing his son with such a place. For,
<>the earth was completely under water. For a long time

<>Na1ra1yan2a (Vis2n2u) could do anything in this matter. So

<NI>2) {%Incarnation.%} Instantly the young one of a Boar
<>jumped out of the nose of Brahma1 through his breath.
<>That divine figure of Boar stood in the air and began to
<>grow. Within a few moments, it became a colossal

<NI>3) {%Incarnation of Boar again.%} The goddess Earth, the
<>deity of earth which was raised to the surface of water,

<HI>VARARUCI. An ancient Indian scholar in astronomy

<NI>1) {%Birth.%} It is stated in Katha1saritsa1gara, Katha1pi1t2ha-

<NI>2) {%Of sharp intelligence.%} Vararuci was born as the son

<NI>As his father died in his childhood, Vararuci was
<>brought up by his mother. She was in great penury

<>came to her house. While they were sitting on the

<NI>3) {%Getting a teacher.%} The guests had actually been

<NI>In the great city of Nandara1ja, there was a great
<>Brahmin named S4an3karasva1mi1. He had two sons

<>The wife of Upavars2a made this sweet food and gave it
<>to Vars2a. When he brought it home, his wife scolded
<>him. Vars2a felt very sorry because of his foolishness.
<>He gave up all his desires and began to worship
<>Kuma1rasva1mi1. Kuma1rasva1mi1 was pleased with him

<>sva1mi1 had ordered him to teach all of this knowledge

<NI>During this period there lived two Brahmins named

<>They were friends. A son was born to each of them.
<>The son of Devasva1mi1 was named Vya1li1. The name of
<>the son of Karambhaka was Indradatta. When Vya1li1

<NI>Vya1li1 said all about these things to the mother of

<NI>Next morning, with the permission of his mother,

<NI>4) {%Marriage.%} Vararuci learned everything from the

<HI>VASIS2T2HA. A hermit who was the son of Brahma1.
<NI>1) {%The three births of Vasis2t2ha.%} Vasis2t2ha with the radiance
<>of Brahma1, is very famous in the Pura1n2as. He had three
<>births.
<NI>i) {%First birth.%}
<NI>a) {%Birth.%} Vasis2t2ha is one of the mental sons of Brahma1.
<>This is the first birth of Vasis2t2ha.
<NI>“Na1rada was born from the lap, Daks2a was born from
<>the right thumb, Vasis2t2ha from the breath (pra1n2a)
<>Bhr2gu from the skin, Kratu from the hand of Brahma1.”
<NI>In this birth, Arundhati1 was the wife of Vasis2t2ha.
<>Arundhati1 was known by the name U1rja1 also. There is
<>a Pura1n2ic story behind the marriage of Vasis2t2ha and
<>Arundhati1.
<NI>In her previous birth the name of Arundhati1 was
<>Sandhya1. She was born from the passion of Brahma1.
<>As soon as she was born she grew up. Seeing her exqui-
<>site beauty the Praja1patis were filled with excitement.
<>Even Brahma1, her father, was some-what excited at her
<>sight. S4iva, who understood this, teased Brahma1.
<>Sandhya1 was ashamed. Even after S4iva, Brahma1, Pra-
<>ja1patis and the others had gone their ways, she remained
<>there blaming her birth. She said to herself: “The mo-
<>ment I was born, I grew up to be a young woman. My
<>father and my brothers looked at me with desire. I
<>also looked at them excitedly. As an atonement for
<>this sin, I will burn my body in fire. I do not want a
<>body desired by my father and brothers. With this
<>decision she went to the mountain Candrabha1ga, which
<>is the source of the river Candrabha1ga1, and began to
<>perform penance. Brahma1 who came to know of this, [Page834-b+ 65]
<>was filled with pity and sent Vasis2t2ha to her. He went
<>there in the form of a Brahmin boy and taught her how
<>to perform penance. After the return of Vasis2t2ha she con-
<>tinued the severe penance to Vis2n2u. Her penance became
<>the subject of talk and wonder everywhere. After a short
<>while Vis2n2u appeared before her sitting on his convey-
<>ance Garud2a. She praised Vis2n2u. Vis2n2u was pleased
<>with her and asked what her desire was. She said:
<>“Lord, creatures should not be sexually excited at their
<>birth. They should have sexual desire only when they
<>are grown up. The three worlds must know that I am
<>chaste. In all my births I should not look at anybody
<>except my husband with sexual desire. The man who
<>looks at me with sexual desire should lose his manliness
<>and become a hermaphrodite.”
<NI>Maha1vis2n2u agreed to her request. It was from that day
<>onwards that sexual desire appeared in creatures in
<>their grown-up stage only, after they have passed the
<>stages of infancy and childhood. Maha1vis2n2u told her.
<>“It is preordained that this body of yours will be burnt
<>in fire. Medha1tithi, (Megha1tithi), the son of Priyavrata
<>is performing the great sacrifice called Jyotis2t2oma which
<>is to be completed in twelve years. It is coming to a
<>close. There is none equal to him because of this sacri-
<>fice. That great hermit's sacrifice is being performed in
<>the basin of this river Candrabha1ga1. Unseen by the
<>hermits, you should go there and get into the fire. Be-
<>cause of my blessing you will be born from that fire as
<>the daughter of Medha1tithi. You should go into the fire
<>thinking of him whom you want to be your husband in
<>this birth.”
<NI>Maha1vis2n2u touched Sandhya1 with the tip of his finger.
<>Sandhya1 walked to the sacrificial hall. Seen by none,
<>she got down into the fire. She was burnt in the blaz-
<>ing fire. By the order of Vis2n2u; the God fire placed
<>Sandhya1 who was burnt in the sacrificial fire, in the
<>Solar region. The sun divided that body into two and
<>placed them in his chariot. The upper portion became
<>the pra1tassandhya1 (dawn) between the day and the
<>night and the lower portion became the Sa1yantana
<>Sandhya1 (the evening twilight). At the end of the
<>sacrifice, from the centre of the sacrificial fire a girl,
<>like the flame of fire rose up. Medha1tithi took that
<>child in his hands and called her Arundhati1. The child
<>became famous throughout the three worlds, as the
<>name stood for the principle that on no reason what-so-
<>ever will righteousness be obstructed. (Rodha means
<>obstruction. So Arundhati1 is one who cannot be obstruct-
<>ed). In some other Pura1n2as Arundhati1 is given as
<>the daughter of Praja1pati Kardama and Devahu1ti.
<NI>b) {%Marriage.%} Arundhati1 grew up in the hermitage
<>of Medha1tithi. Candrabha1ga1 holy bath which was the
<>playfield of Arundhati1, is even today, known as Arun-
<>dhati1ti1rtha. Arundhati1 became five years of age. Brahma1
<>saw her when she was playing on the ground after hav-
<>ing taken her bath. At the instruction of Brahma1,
<>Arundhati1 was entrusted to Sa1vitri1 and Bahula1 for
<>education. Sa1vitri1 is the wife of the Sun. Arundhati1
<>lived in Ma1nasa lake with Sa1vitri1, Ga1yatri1, Bahula1,
<>Sarasvati1, Drupada1 and such other celestial women
<>and completed her education. One day Arundhati1
<>happened to see Vasis2t2ha who was shining with radi-
<>ance. They fell in love with each other. Parents and
<>relatives and the elders came to know of this. Sa1vitri
<>patting Arundhati1 blessed her to become the wife of [Page835-a+ 64]
<>Vasis2t2ha. The marriage of Arundhati1 with Vasis2t2ha was
<>conducted in the presence of the Gods.
<NI>c) {%Sons.%} Seven sons, named Citraketu, Purocis, Viraca,
<>Mitra, Ulban2a, Vasubhr2dya1na and Dyuma1n were born
<>to Vasis2t2ha by Arundhati1. All the seven of them were
<>Brahmars2is.
<NI>{%d) The meaning of the names Vasis2t2ha and Arundhati1.%} The
<>meaning of the name Vasis2t2ha is given by Vasis2t2ha
<>himself as follows:--
<NI>I am known as Vasis2t2ha for two reasons. I am ‘Vasu-
<>ma1n’. The S4rutis say that Air, Earth etc. are Vasus.
<>I have become Vasis2t2ha because I have brought under
<>control the Vasus beginning with An2ima1 (the power
<>of reducing the body to an atom). See what Arun-
<>dhati1 herself says, about the meaning of the name
<>Arundhati1.
<NI>“I consider mountains, earth and heaven as elements
<>in which I live, only after considering my hus-
<>band as the element in which I live. My husband
<>is the first and foremost element in my life. Moreover
<>I conform (anurodha) with the mind of my husband.
<>So know me as Arundhati1.”
<NI>{%e) Conjugal fidelity of Arundhati1.%} The Saptars2is (the seven
<>hermits) once left Arundhati1 alone in a forest and went
<>to the Mountain Hima1layas to gather fruits and roots.
<>In those days, due to severe summer, the earth
<>became a wilderness. So the hermits lived in the
<>Hima1layas. Arundhati1 all alone did penance in the
<>forest. On one day S4iva took the form of a Brahmin and
<>going near Arundhati1 requested her for alms. She rep-
<>lied: “There are only Ziziphus fruits here, and nothing
<>else to eat.” The Brahmin asked her to boil them. She
<>placed the pot of Ziziphus fruits on the oven and sat
<>there hearing the good stories told by the Brahmin. Thus
<>without thinking about her hunger or thirst she sat there
<>for twelve years hearing the stories narrated by the
<>Brahmin. When the hermits returned from Hima1layas,
<>S4iva assumed his original form and said, “Hermits!
<>This woman, sitting in the hermitage, has acquired
<>more penance than you have acquired in the Hima1layas.
<>Good woman! What boon do you want?” She
<>requested that that place should be known as the holy
<>place called ‘Badarapacana (cooking of Ziziphus fruits).
<>S4iva allowed it. Even today that place is considered
<>a holy place.
<NI>f) {%Death.%} When so many devas were dead at the sacri-
<>fice of Daks2a, Vasis2t2ha also died along with them.
<>Arundhati1 followed her husband. After death both of
<>them entered the firmament and became two stars.
<NI>g) {%Seeing Arundhati1.%} In India there is a custom of show-
<>ing the women, the star Arundhati1. Arundhati1 is the
<>first of the women who took only one husband in her life.
<>The meaning of this custom is this that this mentality of
<>Arundhati1 should be acquired by the married women
<>of India. Moreover, if the star stands in front of the star
<>Vasis2t2ha, it is considered to forebode calamities in the
<>world. (Ka1lika1 Pura1n2a).
<NI>ii) {%Second birth.%}
<NI>{%General information.%} Vasis2t2ha who died at the sacrifice
<>of Daks2a took birth again from the sacrificial fire of
<>Brahma1. Aks2ama1la1 was the wife of this Vasis2t2ha.
<>Aks2ama1la1 was the rebirth of Arundhati1. So, in some
<>Pura1n2as, both are shown as one. This birth of Vasis2-
<>t2ha was terminated by the curse of emperor Nimi of [Page835-b+ 65]
<>the Iks2va1ku dynasty. (For details see under Nimi).
<NI>(iii) {%Third birth.%} In the third birth Vasis2t2ha was born
<>from a pot as the son of Mitra1varun2as. In this birth
<>Vasis2t2ha was the brother of Agastya. (For detailed
<>story see under Agastya, para 2). In this birth the
<>wife of Vasis2t2ha was an Arundhati1, who was the sister
<>of Na1rada. Thus according to the Pura1n2as, it took
<>three births for Vasis2t2ha to complete his life. It is
<>difficult to ascertain, in which particular birth, a parti-
<>cular story, stated in the Pura1n2as, took place. It is
<>probable that a large number of episodes might have
<>taken place in the second and third births.
<NI>Stories connected with the life of Vasis2t2ha are given
<>below:
<NI>2) {%Vasis2t2ha and Vis4va1mitra.%} Vasis2t2ha and Vis4va1mitra
<>were two herm its who quarrelled with each other through-
<>out their lives. The quarrel between Vasis2t2ha a
<>Brahmin hermit and Vis4va1mitra a royal hermit, is
<>given below:
<NI>(i) {%Reason for the enmity.%} Vis4va1mitra was a King who
<>cared much for the welfare of his subjects. Once he
<>went with his army to hunt. He became tired by the
<>hunt and reached the hermitage of Vasis2t2ha who
<>welcomed them with hospitality. He told them that
<>food would be ready when they returned after a bath.
<>The King and his men bathed quickly and when they
<>returned, a grand feast was ready for so many thou-
<>sands. The King was in great perplexity. After the
<>meals Vis4va1mitra approached the hermit Vasis2t2ha
<>and asked him how he got such a grand feast ready.
<>He replied that the cow Ka1madhenu in his hermitage was
<>capable of granting any wish. The king desired to have
<>the cow. He asked the hermit to exchange the cow for
<>a crore of ordinary cows. Vasis2t2ha did not agree to
<>this. Vis4va1mitra said that the noble and superior
<>things of the country belonged to the King. The hermit
<>did not agree to that also. Finally Vis4va1mitra was
<>about to take away the cow by force. Thus the quarrel
<>began. Understanding the wish of Vasis2t2ha Ka1madhenu
<>held her horns and tail up and stood as a fierce
<>and cruel figure. From the various limbs of the cow so
<>many thousands of warriors jumped out and a fierce
<>battle ensued in which the hundred sons and the huge
<>army of Vis4va1mitra met with defeat. At last Vis4va1mitra
<>tried to launch a direct attack against Vasis2t2ha. But
<>the arrows of Vis4va1mitra were changed to flowers when
<>they touched the body of Vasis2t2ha. At last the King
<>admitted that the power of the penance of a Brahmin
<>hermit was the real power and he admitted defeat from
<>Vasis2t2ha. From that day onwards a deep-rooted,
<>hatred against Vasis2t2ha arose in the heart of Vis4va1mitra.
<>He left the administration of his Kingdom in the hands
<>of his relatives and went to the south where he erected
<>a hermitage and began to do severe penance. He acquir-
<>ed great powers of penance and became a royal hermit
<>of immense attainments and the quarrel between the
<>two great hermits Vasis2t2ha and Vis4va1mitra began.
<>(Va1lmi1ki Ra1ma1yan2a, Ba1la Ka1n2d2a, 5 sargas from 51).
<NI>(ii) {%Second confrontation.%} The next contest between the two
<>hermits was due to the king Tris4an3ku of the Solar
<>dynasty. Tris4an3ku wanted bodily attainment of heaven.
<>Vasis2t2ha tried to discourage the king. Vis4va1mitra took
<>up the matter. He began to perform a sacrifice to lift
<>up the king bodily to heaven, and Tris4an3ku began to
<>rise up higher and higher. But Indra did not allow him [Page836-a+ 65]
<>to enter bodily into the heaven. At last Vis4va1mitra, by
<>the power of his penance created an artificial heaven
<>midway between the heaven and the earth and placed
<>Tris4an3ku in that heaven. With this the gap between
<>the two hermits widened. (For more details see under
<>Tris4an3ku).
<NI>(iii) {%Third confrontation.%} By the blessing of Varun2a, a son
<>named Lohita was born to Haris4candra. He had promis-
<>ed Varun2a to sacrifice his son Lohita. But Lohita
<>came to know of this and he left the palace. Haris4can-
<>dra was in a difficult situation. Vasis2t2ha advised him
<>to buy a son and to sacrifice him. Accordingly a Brah-
<>min boy named S4unas4s4epha was bought. Vasis2t2ha
<>decided to sacrifice him. Vis4va1mitra said that he could

<NI>6) {%Curbing the arrogance of Silk-cotton tree.%} Long ago a
<>silk-cotton tree grew up on the top of the Hima1layas.

<HI>VEDA (S).
<NI>1) {%Introduction.%} The root ‘Vid’ in Sanskrit means ‘to
<>know’. The books composed of the knowledge of the [Page842-a+ 65]
<>A1ryans, collected and compiled were called the Vedas.
<NI>2) {%The origin and importance of the Vedas.%} It is said that
<>Brahma1 was the creator of the Vedas. Many say that,
<>for the performance of sacrifices Brahma1 created from
<>Agni (fire), Va1yu (Wind) and Ravi (the Sun), the
<>three Vedas R2g, Yajus and Sa1man which are eternal and
<>in accordance with regulations.
<NI>The Vedas have two sides, the spiritual and the mun-
<>dane. Moreover all the explanations of the Vedas
<>from the Bra1hman2as to the Bha1s2ya of Sa1yan2a, pertain
<>to sacrifices. The literary meaning of Veda is mundane.
<>Considering these two points and the facts that they are
<>religious books and that they reveal the mental and
<>social outlooks of the early A1ryans, and as the origin of
<>all the thoughts of Indians, all the Vedas, especially
<>R2gveda, hold a lofty place.
<NI>3) {%Parts of the Vedas.%} Maha1vis2n2u incarnated as Vya1sa
<>in Dva1para Yuga and divided the Vedas. The first
<>Veda consisted of four pa1das and a hundred thousand
<>granthas. Vya1sa divided it into four parts known as,
<>R2gveda, Yajurveda, Sa1maveda and Atharvaveda.
<>The sage and seer Vya1sa thus created by R2g, “Hautra”
<>(a collection of lyrics in praise of different Gods, to be
<>recited by the priest styled the ‘hotr2’), by Yajus
<>“A1dhvaryava”, (a book of sacrificial prayer, of prose
<>formulas to be uttered by the ‘Adhvaryu’ priest, who
<>performed the manual work involved in a sacrifice), by
<>Sa1man, “Audga1tra”, (Songs meant to be sung at the
<>Soma sacrifice by a special class of priests ‘Udga1tr2’) and
<>by Atharva “Brahmatva”, (a collection of songs, spells
<>and incantations, for the healing of disease, the restora-
<>tion of harmony, the exorcism of evil spirits and to
<>celebrate the power and omniscience of God) and
<>established them separately. Paila, a scholar in R2g-
<>veda, and a disciple of Vya1sa, gave the original Veda
<>to Indrapramiti and its Sam3hita1 (collections) to Ba1s2kala
<>as gifts. Ba1s2kala divided the Sam3hita1 into four, and
<>gave each of them to Baudhya and others. Yajurveda
<>was divided into twentyfour branches. They were com-
<>posed by Vais4ampa1yana of extraordinary intelligence,
<>a disciple of Vya1sa. Ka1n2d2as (Chapters) such as Va1ja-
<>saneya etc. were composed later by hermits such as
<>Ya1jn5avalkya and others in the form of Smr2tis (tradition,
<>as handing down only the tradition derived from an-
<>cient sages, to whom the Vedas were ‘revealed’).
<>Jaimini the disciple of Vya1sa, divided Sa1maveda into
<>different branches. Sumantu and Sukarma1 compiled
<>separate Sam3hita1s (collections) from them. Sukarma1
<>composed thousand Sam3hita1s. Sumantu the disciple
<>of Vya1sa took the Atharvaveda and taught it to
<>thousands of Paippala1da disciples. By the blessings of
<>Vya1sa, Su1ta made the Pura1n2a Sam3hita1 (the collection
<>of Pura1n2as). (Agni Pura1n2a, Chapter 150).
<NI>4) {%Branches af the Vedas.%} It has already been mentioned
<>that the Vedas are four in number called R2g, Yajus,
<>Sa1ma and Atharva. Each of these Vedas has branches
<>called Sam3hita1s (collections) and Bra1hman2as (treatises
<>relating to prayer and sacrificial ceremony). A1ran2yakas
<>are appendices to the Bra1hman2as. Upanis2ads (secret
<>or esoteric doctrines) are appendices of the A1ran2yakas.
<>Thus each of the Vedas has Sam3hita1s, Bra1hman2as,
<>A1ran2yakas and Upanis2ads. All these are, in a way, ex-
<>positions of the Vedas. In all these expositions there
<>are numberless Su1ktas. All these taken together are
<>called Vedic literature. [Page842-b+ 65]
<>In the Sam3hita1s there are lyrics in praise of different gods.
<>All these are spells and incantations (mantras) in the
<>form of songs. The under-currents of all these spells are
<>Vedas and stories from the Vedas. Generally speaking
<>the Bra1hman2as contain prose texts giving practical
<>observations on sacrifice which are mentioned in the
<>songs of praise. Here and there stories from Pura1n2as
<>and epics occur. The A1ran2yakas (forest-texts) got that
<>name, because they are books of instruction to be given
<>in the forest or writings meant for wood-dwelling her-
<>mits. As they contained esoteric spells and incanta-
<>tions which might cause injury even to those who were
<>not concerned with them instruction in them was not
<>given in towns or villages. The contents of the A1ran2y-
<>akas are the allegorical signification of the rites and
<>sacrifices and the mystic meaning of the Vedas.
<NI>It has been mentioned that the Upanis2ads are append-
<>ices of the A1ran2yakas. Still there is not much differ-
<>ence between the two and hence they cannot be separat-
<>ed from one another so easily. The Upanis2ads are
<>called Veda1ntas, (The aim and completion of the
<>Vedas), because they are the end of the Vedas. The
<>Veda1ntas belong to the later period of the Vedic age.
<>Instruction in Veda1ntas was given only after completing
<>the study of the mantras (Vedas) and the Bra1hman2as.
<>The Upanis2ads contain philosophical speculations about
<>the conception of Brahman and the Vedas. The word
<>Veda includes the Veda1n3gas also. Veda1n3gas (Ancillaries
<>of the Vedas) are S4iks2a1 (phonetics), Vya1karan2a
<>(grammar), Chandas (metrics), Nirukta (etymology),
<>Joytis2a (astronomy), and Kalpa (ritual). At first
<>instruction is given in the study of Brahman and the
<>study of Vedas. When more discussions and expositions
<>on them are needed, the study of Bra1hman2as and
<>A1ran2yakas are resorted to. In course of time the
<>Bra1hman2as and A1ran2yakas, which contain discussions
<>and expositions of the Vedas became independent
<>branches of study under these names. That is why they
<>contain mainly prose texts.
<NI>There are one lakh of mantras or spells and incanta-
<>tions in all the four Vedas taken together. They are
<>for blessing everybody and to make the four objects of
<>life easily attainable. Sa1n3khya1yana and A1s4vala1yana
<>sorted and grouped the mantras. Accordingly there
<>are two thousand one hundred and ten mantras known
<>as Bra1hman2as. Dvaipa1yana and other hermits have
<>stated the number of granthas (verses) in R2gveda. It
<>is said that there are one thousand nine hundred and
<>ninety nine mantras in Yajurveda. There are one
<>thousand eightysix branches also. The branches in
<>Yajus are known by the names Ka1n2vi1, Ma1dhyandini1,
<>Kat2hi1, Madhyakat2hi1, Maitra1yan2i1, Taittiri1ya, Vais4am-
<>pa1yanika1 and so on.
<NI>In Sa1ma Veda there are branches such as Kauthumi1,
<>A1tharvan2a1yini1 and so on; and songs such as A1ran2yakam,
<>Uktham, U1ham and son on. The number of Sa1mavedic
<>verses are nine thousand four hundred and twenty-
<>five.
<NI>Sumantu, Jan5jali, S4loka1yani, S4aunaka, Pippala1da,
<>Mun5jakes4a and such others were responsible for the
<>sorting and grouping of the mantras in the Atharva-
<>veda. Altogether there are one thousand six hundred
<>Upanis2ads. (Agni Pura1n2a, Chapter 271).
<NI>5) {%Expositions of the Vedas.%} The religion of the A1ryans
<>became an established one when Vya1sa had created the [Page843-a+ 65]
<>Vedasam3hita1s. The aim of Vya1sa was to bring about
<>uniformity in the religious observances by performing
<>rites and rituals, religious ceremonies such as sacrifices
<>etc. without any flaw. Following this a very wide
<>Vedic literature grew up. The study of the Vedas,
<>critical review of meaning, the connection between
<>mantras and tantras (Chants and rituals), Grammar,
<>etymology, all these became inevitable. As the Vedas
<>could be looked at from different points of view, from
<>very early days, various types of expositions of the
<>Vedas came out. Seven types of commentaries,
<>Nairukta, Ya1jn5ika, Vaiya1karan2a Jyautis2a, Sa1mprada1yika
<>A1dhya1tmika, Aitiha1sika (pertaining to etymology,
<>sacrifice, grammar astronomy, customs of a tribe,
<>Bra1hma or Spiritual legends and ancient lore) were
<>the prominent among them. When the westerners
<>began research work in the Vedas, another branch of
<>literature also took form, known as the A1gamikas
<>(the historical). Even in the time of Ya1ska, who
<>was an authority on Nirukta (etymology) the Vedas
<>were expounded on the basis of legends and ancient
<>lore. Hints to this effect are seen in Ya1ska's works.
<>Mention is made about other types of expositions also,
<>in them. The last book of importance in the Sa1mpra-
<>da1yika type of exposition, was Veda1rthapraka1s4a, of
<>Sa1yan2a. But the commentary of Skandasva1mi1, the
<>books R2garthadipika1 and Udgi1thabha1s2ya of Ma1dhava1-
<>ca1rya etc. have spread the sa1mprada1yika type of
<>speculations in India. There is another cult in India
<>which believes that everything seen in the Vedas is
<>spiritual and that the spells and incantations are
<>esoteric.
<NI>6) {%The gods of the Vedas.%} All the gods known today
<>are not found in the Vedas. Even those who are found
<>do not have the prominence that is given to them now.
<>For example, the deity Vis2n2u, worshipped as one of
<>the three godheads today, is not as omnipotent as the
<>Indra of the Vedas. Though Vis2n2u is praised in five
<>spells in R2gveda, when compared with other deities,
<>he was not of much prominence. In the Vedas the
<>incarnation of Va1mana is not given much importance.
<>Even though Rudra is a recognized deity and mention
<>occurs about Kapardi1, in the Vedas, there is not a song
<>of praise of S4iva in the R2gveda. There is no mention
<>at all, about the worship of the Phallus, Devi1 and so
<>on in the Vedas. The Vedas celebrate the Omniscience
<>of Varun2a, Indra, Agni, Mitra, the Maruts and so on.
<>The lustre of Indra was gradually dimmed with the
<>efflux of time and he became a mere libertine in the
<>Pura1n2as. The importance of many deities such as
<>Varun2a, Agni, Mitra, As4vin and so on was greatly dimi-
<>nished in the Pura1n2as. Thirtythree deities pertaining
<>to Earth, Ether and Sky are praised in the Vedas.
<NI>7) {%The rites concerning instruction in Vedas.%} Manu has
<>given certain instructions as to how the teaching of
<>Vedas should be conducted.
<NI>8) {%The teachers of Veda.%} See under Guruparampara1.
<NI>9) {%The period of the Vedas.%} The Indians believe that the
<>spells and incantations and the Bra1hman2as are not man-
<>made, but are revelations by God. So they are con-
<>sidered to be beginningless and endless. The hermits
<>are considered to be seers of the spells. It is mentioned
<>“Mantradras2t2a1rah2 na tu Karta1rah2”. (They are seers
<>of Mantra, not makers). In the opinion of one party,
<>according to this maxim, it is not necessarry to search [Page843-b+ 64]
<>for the creators or the period of creation, of mantras.
<>They hold that only the Su1tras (thread, clue, guide,
<>rule, aphorism) are made by man.
<NI>The westerners and the modern thinkers of India do
<>not agree completely with this view. They believe
<>that the early A1ryans who entered India, first settled
<>down in the Punjab and that the local civilization which
<>they had assumed, broke out as songs of praise. In
<>course of time, these songs of Praise took the form of
<>R2gveda mantras (saying, song, formula). In the begin-
<>ning there was only one Veda. Many believe that this
<>state continued up to B.C. 1500. It is a fact universally
<>acknowledged, that this Vedic literature is the most
<>ancient literature of the world. There is difference of
<>opinion as to the period of origin of this Vedic literature.
<>Prof. Macdonell and Prof. Jacobi are foremost among
<>those who have made their opinions. In the opinion
<>of Prof. Macdonell, the Vedic literature originated in
<>the period between B.C. 1500 and 1200. But Jacobi's
<>opinion is that all the Vedas were made before B.C.
<>4000.

<NI>Vena grew up as a great sinner. A story occurs in
<>Padma Pura1n2a about an incident which caused Vena
<>to become a great sinner.
<NI>The story says that Suni1tha1 was the mother of Vena. In
<>her play she used to imitate her father's job which was
<>hurting others. One day when she went to the forest
<>for play with her maids she saw Sus4an3kha the son of
<>a Gandharva named Gi1takola1hala. That youth who

<NI>She told him “My father will beat everybody in the

<NI>She again went to the forest and struck him with a

<NI>“You wicked girl! When you become a house-holder

<NI>3) {%The wicked rule of Vena.%} The hermits anointed Vena
<>as the King. He became lord of the whole earth. He

<NI>The hermits became angry. They all gathered together

<HI>VIGRAHA III. (Image).
<NI>1) {%General information.%} God, who is not discernible to
<>the outward senses, is given embodiment and consecrat-
<>ed in places of worship by people. These figures are
<>called Vigrahas (idols or images). People worship
<>S4a1lagra1ma, (a kind of ammonite found in the river
<>Gan2d2aki1), Ba1n2alin3ga (Phallus), mystical diagrams,
<>animals, birds, trees, rivers, lakes, places of death etc.
<>and so many other things.
<NI>2) {%The different kinds of Vigrahas.%} Vigrahas are of three
<>groups. They are:-(1) Mysterious (2) Evident-mysteri-
<>ous (3) Evident. S4a1lagra1ma, Phallus etc. belong to the
<>group mysterious. The Mukhalin3ga, considered to be
<>the image of Trimu1rti (Brahma1, Vis2n2u, S4iva) in the
<>Elephanta cave, belongs to the group Evident. The
<>image of Phallus is Evident-mysterious. In the first,
<>there is no form or figure. In the second there are parts
<>of the figure. The image which shows the entire figure
<>is Evident.
<NI>Some gods and goddesses possess two appearances,
<>peaceful and fierce. Those who wish to succeed in
<>performing cruel deeds and to vanquish enemies, wor-
<>ship fierce gods whereas those who wish for peace,
<>worship peaceful Gods. Vis4varu1pa, (assuming all
<>shapes), Narasim3ha (the man-lion), Vat2apatras4a1yi1 (as
<>lying on banyan-leaf) and Paras4ura1ma are fierce forms
<>of Vis2n2u. Destroying Ka1ma (cupid) Gaja and Tripura
<>are fierce forms of S4iva worshipped by some people.
<>Generally temples with images in this form are erected
<>outside the village or city.
<NI>Owing to the differences, in the making and the mater-
<>ials used, the images are divided into three groups. [Page852-a+ 64]
<>They are portraits, Half-portraits and corrupted
<>portraits. The whole of the figure will be made in
<>(portraits) citras. In half-citras only the front view
<>will be completed. Corrupted Citras are images done
<>on the wall or rock.
<NI>3) {%Main images.%} Main images are mostly S4aivite or
<>Vais2n2avite. There will be one or two other images.
<>Worship of Devi1 (Goddess) is one of them. The S4aivi-
<>tes will worship Pa1rvati1 also after S4iva and the Vais2n2a-
<>vites Maha1laks2mi1 also after Vis2n2u In South India the
<>worshippers are S4aivites and Vais2n2avites.
<NI>4) {%S4aivites.%} In India a large number of people worship
<>S4iva. There is not much difference in the mode of wor-
<>ship of these various people. There are worships which
<>are in accordance with the Vedas and which are not.
<>Forms of worship which are Sa1ttvika (of goodness) and
<>which are not, could be seen. The S4aiva worship called
<>Paras4upada is very ancient. The phallus at Gud2imalla
<>is considered to be as old as B.C. 2nd century. From
<>this it could be inferred how old, the S4aivite worship is
<>in India.
<NI>5) {%The S4aivite images.%} Of the emblems denoting S4iva,
<>the most important is the Phallus, which is of two kinds,
<>movable and immovable. Risen by itself and or erected
<>and set firm and consecrated inside temples are immov-
<>able; that which is made of earth, metal, jewel, wood
<>or stone, is movable. There are Phalluses made for the
<>time being. They are fixed on platforms or pedestals.
<>They are of different sizes and shapes. The Phallus is
<>made of male stone and the pedestal of female stone.
<NI>6) {%The portions of S4iva.%} There are various kinds of images
<>meant to reveal various attributes of S4iva. Lin3godbhava
<>(originated from Phallus), Candras4ekhara, Raudra,

<>ntaka (killing Ka1ma or Cupid), Gaja1ri (enemy of Gaja),

<>the figures of blessing Can2d2es4a, Vis2n2u, Nandi1s4vara,
<>Vighnes4a and Arjuna also. There are a large number

<>explanation, knowledge, yoga (or meditation, contem-

<NI>7) {%The Devas (gods) connected with S4iva.%} Among the gods
<>connected with S4iva, first place is given to Gan2apati.

<NI>In South India temples dedicated to Gan2apati are not
<>scarce. The position of Gan2apati is at the entrance of

<NI>There are images of Gan2apati in the postures of stand-

<HI>VIJAYADAS4AMI1. A festival of Indians. As this festival
<>is celebrated for nine nights from the 1st to the 9th in the
<>bright lunar fortnight of the month of Kanni (Sep-
<>tember-October) it is known as Navara1tri (Nine nights)
<>and as it continues up to Das4ami1 (the tenth night) it
<>is called Dasra. The Hindus believe that the Vijaya-
<>das4ami1 (the victorious tenth) was the day on which
<>Devi1 Durga1 killed Mahis2a1sura and got victory. So this
<>day is considered to be a suitable moment to begin the
<>learning of all the arts which would enable one to carry
<>on a successful life. Sarasvati1 is considered the trans-
<>figuration of Durga1. As people became less superstiti-
<>ous, they began to consider the story of killing Mahis2a1-
<>sura as a metaphorical saying, to mean the killing of
<>ignorance. So the day of victory of Devi1 Durga1 (the same
<>as Sarasvati1) is considered to be the auspicious moment
<>for the beginning of learning. The warrior places his
<>weapons, the man of literature his books and pen, the
<>musician his musical instruments, at the feet of Devi1 and
<>with devotion and worship receives them back from
<>Devi1 on the Vijayadas4ami1 day at an auspicious
<>moment.
<NI>This is a festival celebrated everywhere in India. In
<>several native states this festival used to be celebrated
<>under the sponsorship of the royal family as a State
<>festival. As it is believed that Mahis2a1sura had lived in
<>Mysore the celebration of Dasra in that State generally
<>is on a grand scale. In Kerala, from olden times this
<>festival was celebrated under the patronage of the Van5ci
<>Royal family.

<>ed the snake tightly round the stomach. Candra who

<>with contempt. At this, Gan2apati got wild and plucked
<>his tusk and throwing it at the moon cursed him. “Let [Page857-a+ 65]
<>nobody look at you on the Gan2apati-festival day.”
<>(Brahmavaivarta Pura1n2a). This story is slightly differ-
<>ent according to Gan2es4a Pura1n2a. That story is, that

<HI>VIS2N2U.
<NI>1) {%General information.%} Brahma1, Vis2n2u and Mahes4vara
<>are the Lords of creation, sustenance and extermination
<>of this perishable universe. These trimu1rtis (three
<>figures) also are perishable. It is said, that one day of
<>Brahma1 will constitute thousand four-fold (catur) yugas
<>and that during the life of Brahma1, fourteen Indras will
<>fall down from heaven and die. This is a Brahma1 age.
<>The ages of two Brahma1s constitute the age of one Vis2n2u.
<>At the end of the age Vis2n2u also will perish. The age
<>of S4iva is double the age of Vis2n2u. S4iva also will perish
<>at the end of his age. (Devi1 Bha1gavata, Skandha 5).
<NI>When everything perishes there comes the deluge (the
<>great flood). After that, for one hundred and twenty
<>Brahma1 years the universe will be desolate and void. In
<>that deep eternal silence, Vis2n2u will be seen sleeping on
<>a banyan leaf on the surface of water. That is the
<>beginning of the next great age. In this stage, Ba1la-
<>mukunda is the name of Maha1vis2n2u. As he remains on
<>Na1ra or water he will be called Na1ra1yan2a also.
<NI>The name Vis2n2u means he who possesses the habit of
<>Vya1pana (To pervade). While Vis2n2u, who has the
<>power to spread his control over everything in whatever
<>condition, lies on the banyan-leaf. From his navel, a
<>lotus-stalk grows up, and on the top of the stalk, in the
<>lotus flower, Brahma1 comes into being. Brahma1 does
<>penance before Vis2n2u and extols him. Maha1vis2n2u confers
<>on Brahma1 the power of creation of the subjects. That
<>Brahma1 perishes along with the deluge and in his place
<>another Brahma1 is born. Thus in the life-time of Vis2n2u
<>two Brahma1s come into being and perish.
<NI>2) {%Beginning.%} In days of yore, when Vis2n2u was lying
<>on the banyan leaf as Ba1la Mukunda, he began to think
<>“Who am I? Who created me? Why? What have I
<>to perform?” -and soon an ethereal voice was heard,
<>“I am everything. Except me, there is nothing eternal.”
<>From behind the voice Maha1devi1 appeared, and said
<>“Look Vis2n2u. What is there to wonder at? Whenever
<>the universe is subject to creation, sustenance and
<>extermination, you have taken origin by the glory of
<>the Almighty. The Almighty or the omnipotence is
<>beyond attributes. But we are all subjected to attributes.
<>Your foremost attribute is Sattva (goodness-purity)
<>Brahma1 whose main attribute is the attribute of rajas
<>(activity-passions), will originate from your navel.
<>From the middle of the brows of that Brahma1, S4iva
<>will be born, whose main attribute is Tamas (inertia
<>darkness). Brahma1, by the power of Tapas (penance)
<>will acquire the power of creation and build the world.
<>You will be the sustainer of that world. S4iva will dest-
<>roy the same world. I am Devi1 Ma1ya1 (Illusion-
<>personified as the wife of Brahman), the great power
<>depending on you for the purpose of creation.” After
<>hearing these words of Devi1, Vis2n2u went into medita-
<>tion and deep sleep of contemplation.
<NI>3) {%Avata1ras (Incarnations).%} When injustice and law-
<>lessness abound in the universe, Vis2n2u will incarnate in
<>the world in various forms and shapes, and will drive
<>away injustice and will reinstate righteousness. The basis
<>and the indeclinable semen virile of all the incarnations,

<>earth. It was the incarnation as a hog to redeem the

<>The third incarnation was taken to create the sages and

<>s4a1stra explaining the ways of observing Karmans.

<>an2as (two hermits) and performed tapas (penance),

<>another occasion, she arose from a lotus-flower which
<>grew up from the sea of Milk. (To know more about
<>the wives Laks2mi1, Gan3ga1 and Sarasvati1, see under
<>Gan3ga1).
<NI>There is none to be mentioned as the legitimate son of
<>Maha1vis2n2u. But Brahma1 is the first that could be
<>imagined as the son of Vis2n2u. Besides, Maha1vis2n2u once
<>created a bright son, by his mind. That son was named [Page865-a+ 64]
<>Virajas. S4a1sta1 is another son of Maha1vis2n2u. S4iva be-
<>came amorous with Mohini1 (fascinating woman)--the
<>form which Maha1vis2n2u took at the time of the churning
<>of the Sea of Milk. They led a short family life as a
<>result of which the son S4a1sta1 was born. (See under
<>S4a1sta1).
<NI>5) {%Curses.%} Maha1vis2n2u had cursed and had been cursed
<>on many an occasion. The most important of them are
<>given below:
<NI>(i) {%The curse of Maha1laks2mi1%} Once Maha1vis2n2u looked
<>into the face of Maha1laks2mi1 and laughed for no reason.
<>Thinking that Maha1vis2n2u had been making fun of her,
<>she cursed him saying “Let your head be severed from
<>the body.”
<NI>At this period an Asura named Hayagri1va had done
<>penance for a thousand years and obtained several boons.
<>One boon was that he should be killed only by a man with
<>the head of a horse. Hayagri1va attacked the devas (gods).
<>Though the gods fought with Hayagri1va for many thou-
<>sands of years they could not kill him. Even Vis2n2u,
<>admitted defeat. Using the bow as a prop to his chin he
<>stood thinking, for years. In the meanwhile white ants
<>began to eat the string of the bow. When the string
<>was broken, the bow straightened with a sudden jerk
<>and the head of Maha1vis2n2u was severed from the trunk
<>and was thrown away. Vis4vakarma1 cut off the head of
<>a horse and joined it to the trunk of Vis2n2u, who instant-
<>ly rose up and killed Hayagri1va. Thus satisfying the
<>need of the gods and making the curse of Laks2mi1 come
<>true, Vis2n2u regained his original form and returned to
<>Vaikun2t2ha. (Devi1 Bha1gavata, Skandha 1).
<NI>(ii) {%The curse of Bhr2gu.%} The Asuras who were defeated in
<>the war with Devas, approached Puloma1, the mother of
<>their teacher-priest S4ukra, and sought protection. Puloma1,
<>was the wife of hermit Bhr2gu. She began to do penance
<>for the destruction of devas. Knowing this Vis2n2u aimed
<>his weapon, the Discus, at her and killed her. Bhr2gu
<>got angry and cursed Vis2n2u to take birth as a man and
<>suffer the grief of separation from his wife for many
<>years. This curse was the first cause of the incarnation
<>of S4ri1 Ra1ma. (For details see under Bhr2gu, Para 4).
<NI>(iii) {%The curse of Vis2n2u.%} Once the handsome King Revan-
<>ta, mounted on the horse Uccais4s4ravas and came to
<>Vaikun2t2ha. Looking at the handsome youth, Laks2mi1
<>stood for a while enchanted by Revanta and his horse.
<NI>Maha1vis2n2u was displeased at this, and cursed her to
<>take birth on the earth as a mare. Accordingly she was
<>born as a mare and when the duration of the curse was
<>over returned to Vaikun2t2ha. (For details see under
<>Ekavi1ra).
<NI>(iv) {%The curse of Vr2nda1.%} See under Ma1ya1s4iva.
<NI>6) {%Contests and wars.%} Wars are very few in the Pura1n2as
<>in which Vis2n2u had not participated directly or indirect-
<>ly. As almost all of them have been dealt with in
<>various places in this book, they are not given here.
<>Only a few of the prominent among them are mentioned
<>here.
<NI>(i) {%Madhukait2abhas.%} Madhu and Kait2abha are two
<>asuras born from the ear-wax of Maha1vis2n2u. They
<>tried to attack Brahma1 and Vis2n2u killed them. (See
<>under Kait2abha).
<NI>(ii) {%Killing of Andhaka.%} Andhaka was a notorious asura.
<>He was the minister of Mahis2a1sura. When war broke
<>out between asuras and Devas, Andhaka caused havoc [Page865-b+ 65]
<>among the devas. At last in the fight with Vis2n2u
<>Andhaka was killed. (Devi1 Bha1gavata, Skandha 5).
<NI>(iii) {%Killing of Vr2tra1sura.%} See under Vr2tra.
<NI>(iv) {%Ra1hu.%} For the story of how Vis2n2u cut into two the
<>asura Ra1hu, see under Amr2tam.
<NI>(v) {%Contest with Brahma1.%} The story of Vis2n2u and
<>Brahma1 making a competitive journey to find out the
<>crest and foot of S4iva, is given with slight variations in
<>most of the Pura1n2as. (For detailed story see under
<>Brahma1, Para 5).
<NI>(vi) {%For the story of how Vis2n2u confronted the asuras Nemi,

<NI>7) {%The weapons and ornaments of Vis2n2u.%} The following
<>are the prominent ornaments and weapons of Vis2n2u.
<NI>(i) {%S4ri1vatsa.%} This is a mark on the chest. It is said that
<>this is the mark imprinted by the angry Bhr2gu who
<>kicked on the chest of Maha1vis2n2u. (See under Bhr2gu).
<NI>(ii) {%Pa1n5cajanya.%} This is a white conch. Even by the
<>touch of this conch man becomes wise. (For further
<>details see under Pan5caja I).
<NI>(iii) {%The Discus Sudars4ana.%} Vajrana1bha is another
<>name of this weapon. Vis2n2u uses this weapon to deal
<>with fierce enemies. This is a wheel with a hole in the
<>centre and thousand arms going out from the centre.
<>The outer edge is sharp. This Sudars4ana Cakra
<>is operated by putting it on the first finger and turning
<>it round, and releasing it at the enemy. Though it is
<>terrible for the wicked and unjust, it forebodes good to
<>good people and so it is Sudars4ana (good to look at).
<NI>(iv) {%Kaumodaki1.%} This is the club. The syllable “Ku”
<>means the earth. Kumodaka means he who delights
<>the earth. He who makes the earth delightful is Vis2n2u.
<>As the club is the property of Kumodaka (Vis2n2u) it is
<>called Kaumodaki1.
<NI>(v) {%Kaustubha.%} This is the jewel of Maha1vis2n2u. (Ku =
<>the Earth. Stubhna1ti = Pervades (spreads). Kustubha =
<>ocean. Kaustubha-obtained from the sea. This jewel
<>obtained from the sea of milk at the time of its churn-
<>ing, is worn by Maha1vis2n2u on his neck. This is a red
<>Jacinth.
<NI>(vi) {%Nandaka.%} This is the sword of Vis2n2u. It is stated
<>in Maha1bha1rata, S4a1nti Parva, Chapter 166, that this
<>sword was obtained from Indra.
<NI>(vii) {%S4a1ran3g.%} This is the name of the bow of Vis2n2u.
<>This is called Vais2n2avaca1pa (the bow of Vis2n2u) also.
<>A description is given in Va1lmi1ki Ra1ma1yan2a, Ba1la-
<>ka1n2d2a, Sarga 25, as to how this bow was obtained. It
<>is as follows:
<NI>Once the Devas made Vis2n2u and S4iva quarrel with each
<>other, to test their might. The fight between the two
<>began. Vis4vakarma1 gave each of them a bow. The bow
<>of Vis2n2u was called Vais2n2avaca1pa; the bow of S4iva
<>was called S4aivaca1pa. This Vais2n2avaca1pa is S4a1rn3ga.
<>Due to the power of S4a1rn3ga, S4iva was defeated in the
<>fight. Getting angry S4iva gave his bow to the King
<>Devara1ta of Videha. It was this bow that S4ri1 Ra1ma
<>broke at the time of the Svayam3vara marriage of Si1ta1.
<NI>After the fight, Vis2n2u gave his bow to R2ci1ka. That bow
<>changed hands from R2ci1ka to Jamadagni and from him
<>to Paras4ura1ma, who presented this bow to S4ri1 Ra1ma on
<>his return after the marriage with Si1ta1.
<NI>(viii) {%Vaijayanti1.%} This is the necklace of Vis2n2u. This
<>necklace, made of five jewels stuck together, is known
<>by the name Vanama1la1, also. Vis2n2u has a charioteer
<>named Da1ruka and four horses named S4aibya, Sugri1va, [Page866-a+ 64]
<>Meghapus2pa and Vala1haka. Garud2a is the conveyance
<>of Vis2n2u. He holds conch, discus, club and lotus in
<>each of his four hands. It is said that the discus was
<>made by Vis4vakarma1 with the dust of the Sun. In
<>Vis2n2u Pura1n2a particular mention is made about the
<>ornaments of Vis2n2u.
<NI>9) {%The names of Vis2n2u.%} The names of Vis2n2u given in

<NI>1) Vis2n2u. He who is spread everywhere.
<NI>2) Na1ra1yan2a. (i) He who lies on water. (na1ram =
<>water). (ii) He who had adopted Na1ra (human body)
<>in incarnations. (iii) He who enters the human society

<NI>3) Kr2s2n2a. (1) of dark complexion. (2) He who does
<>Kars2an2a (pulling or dragging) on the agha (sin) of

<NI>4) Vaikun2t2ha. (1) The son of Vikun2t2ha1. There is an
<>incarnation as such. (2) At the time of creation twenty-
<>three Tattvas (essences-elements) did not join with one
<>another. So Vis2n2u joined earth to water, ether to air
<>and air to fire; Thus their individual existence was
<>made Vikun2tha-prevented. By achieving this he became
<>Vaikun2t2ha. (3) Vikun2t2ha means wisdom (knowledge).
<>So Vaikun2t2ha is he who has acquired knowledge. (4)

<NI>11) {%Other details%} (i) Mention about Maha1vis2n2u occurs

<>incarnation of Va1mana or Maha1bali. R2gveda gives
<>Maha1vis2n2u only the position of a younger brother of
<>Indra. That is why the author of Amarakos4a has given
<>Vis2n2u synonyms such as Upendra, Indra1varaja etc.
<NI>(ii) Maha1vis2n2u was one of those who came to see

<>S4iva).

<NI>(iv) Maha1vis2n2u gave Subrahman2ya the necklace Vaija-
<>yanti1. (M.B. S4alya Parva, Chapter 45, Stanza 49).
<NI>(v) It is stated in Maha1bha1rata, Sabha1 Parva, Chapter

<>Brahma1. [Page867-a+ 65]
<NI>(vi) Maha1vis2n2u showed grace to Uparicara vasu. (M.B.
<>S4a1nti Parva, Chapter 337, Stanza 33).
<NI>(vii) Maha1vis2n2u once took birth as the son of Aditi.
<>From that day onwards he got the name A1ditya also. (For

<HI>VIS2N2UCITTA. A noble Vais2n2avite devotee, who lived
<>in Tamil Nadu. He lived in Villiputtur. It is said that
<>he was the incarnation of Garud2a. Vis2n2ucitta had ano-
<>ther name Periya1lva1r. A1n2d2a1l who was famous among

<NI>Vis2n2ucitta sang holy hymns in praise of the beloved

<NI>Once at Villiputtur, while he was getting beds ready to

<HI>VIS2N2UDA1SA. A Vais2n2avite devotee who lived in ancient
<>days. The story of this devotee who defeated his king
<>Cola in devotion to Vis2n2u, is given in Padma Pura1n2a,
<>Uttara Khan2d2a, Chapter 110. The story is as follows.
<NI>In days of old there was a king named Cola in Ka1n5ci1-
<>pura. It was because of his reign that the country got
<>the name Cola. He had performed several sacrifices.
<>On the banks of the river Ta1mraparn2i1, stood his golden
<>Yu1pas (pegs on which sacrificial animals were tied)
<>that the place looked like Caitraratha.
<NI>Once the king went to the temple and worshipped
<>Vis2n2u by offering flowers of gold and jewels such as
<>chalcedony and prostrated before Vis2n2u and rose up.
<>At that time a Brahmin named Vis2n2uda1sa from his own
<>city came there to worship, with holy basil and water
<>as offerings. He worshipped with the leaves and flower-
<>bunches of holy basil. Because of his worship by holy
<>basil, the king's worship by jewels, was dimmed. The
<>emperor got angry and said, “Vis2n2uda1sa, you are a poor
<>man who does not know how to worship Vis2n2u. What
<>merit has your worship of holy basil after mine of
<>jewels?” Both began to contest on this point. At last the
<>king said “Let us see who between us will get oneness
<>with Vis2n2u first, you or I”
<NI>After saying this the king went to his palace. He appoint-
<>ed Mudgala the high priest and began to perform a
<>sacrifice to Vis2n2u. The sacrifice was going on with
<>pomp and festivities. Vis2n2uda1sa also was immersed in
<>devotion to Vis2n2u to the best of his abilities.
<NI>Once Visn2uda1sa, after his usual prayer and meditation
<>prepared rice-food. But somebody took away the cook-
<>ed rice unseen by Vis2n2uda1sa. Fearing that he would
<>miss the time for his evening prayer, he did not think
<>of cooking food again. Next day also he cooked food
<>and went for evening prayer. On that day also the rice
<>was stolen. This continued. One day after cooking the
<>food, Vis2n2uda1sa waited close by in a hidden corner. He
<>saw a low-caste man who was a mere skeleton because of [Page867-b+ 65]
<>famine, stealing the cooked rice and feeling pity on him
<>he said, “Stop, stop. How can you eat it without any oily
<>thing? See, take this ghee also.” Saying so he drew
<>near. The out-caste was terrified at this and ran away.
<>On the way he stumbled and fell. Vis2n2uda1sa ran to
<>the spot and fanned him with his cloth. When he rose
<>up the figure in the place of the low-caste was that of
<>the real S4ri1 Na1ra1yan2a with conch, discus and club held
<>in his hands. Because of devotion Vis2n2uda1sa stood be-
<>numbed. While the King Cola and the people were look-
<>ing on, Vis2n2uda1sa got into the divine Vima1na and went
<>to the world of Vis2n2u.
<HI>VIS2N2UDATTA. Son of the Brahmin named Vasudatta.
<>The story of Vis2n2udatta is quoted to prove that bad
<>omens at the beginning of a journey is a warning that
<>the journey would not be fruitful and that it would be
<>rather dangerous.
<NI>When Vis2n2udatta became sixteen years old he decided
<>to go to the city of Valabhi1 for his education. Seven Brah-
<>min boys of his age gathered together and joined him.
<>Deciding not to separate from each other, they started for
<>Valabhi1, without the knowledge of their parents. When
<>they proceeded a little further they saw a bad omen.
<>Vis2n2udatta stood undecided, but the others pressed him
<>on and they continued their journey. Next day by even-
<>ing they reached a village of forest tribes. After walking
<>through the village they reached the house of a woman.
<>They got her permission to stay there for the night.
<>They all lay in a corner. Immediately all slept. Vis2n2u-
<>datta alone lay awake. When the night advanced, a
<>man entered the house. The woman and the man
<>talked for a while and carried on sexual sports, and
<>they lay together and slept. A light was burning in the
<>room. Vis2n2udatta saw everything through the cleavage
<>of the shutters, and thought. “I am sorry that we have
<>come to this house. He is not her husband. Sure! she is
<>a harlot.” As he was thinking thus, foot-steps were
<>heard in the courtyard. A young man fixed his
<>servants in their places. Then he entered the house and
<>saw Vis2n2udatta and his friends. The new-comer was
<>also a forest-man. He had a sword in his hand. He was
<>the owner of the house. Vis2n2udatta said that they were
<>travellers. When he heard it, without saying anything
<>he got inside and saw his wife sleeping with her lover.
<>With the sword in his hand, he cut off the head of the
<>lover. He did not kill the woman, who did not know
<>that her lover was killed. The forester laid the sword
<>down and lay in the same bed and slept. The light was
<>burning.
<NI>After a while the woman woke up, and saw her hus-
<>band who had cut her lover into two. She stood up
<>quickly and took the trunk of her lover and placed it
<>on her shoulder and taking the head in one hand, went
<>out and hid them in the pile of ashes. Then she return-
<>ed and lay down. Vis2n2udatta had followed her steal-
<>thily and seen what she had done. He also returned and
<>sat in the midst of his friends. She rose up and took the
<>sword of her husband and killed him with it. Then
<>coming out she cried aloud. “Oh dear! These travellers
<>have killed my husband.” The servants woke up and
<>came to the house and saw their master lying dead.
<>They tried to attack Vis2n2udatta and his friends.
<>Vis2n2udatta told them everything that he had seen, and
<>showed them the head and the trunk of her lover, hid-
<>den in the ashes. When they saw this they understood [Page868-a+ 64]
<>everything. They tried the woman. At last she admitted
<>the crime. They expelled her and drove her away. After
<>this the travellers returned to their homes. (Katha1sarit-
<>sa1gara, Madanaman5cuka1lambaka, Taran3ga 6).

<>ed by offering flower, on the feet on the first day, on
<>the navel on the second day, on the eyes on the third

<NI>15). {%Vis4va1mitra and R2gveda.%} R2gveda, Man2dala 5, was
<>composed by the Vis4va1mitra-family. Variations are
<>observed in the two versions of statements about Vis4va1-
<>mitra, occurring in R2gveda and the Pura1n2as. The con-
<>frontations between Vasis2t2ha and Vis4va1mitra occur in
<>R2gveda also. The last four sections of Su1kta 15 of
<>R2gveda, Man2d2ala 3, Anuva1ka 4, are meant to scold
<>Vasis2t2ha. Here Vis4va1mitra curses Vasis2t2ha's family in
<>various ways. In the ‘Annotations of Sa1yan2a’, mention
<>is made that the disciples of Vasis2t2ha freed Vis4va1mitra
<>from the vow of silence, and that instantly these mantras
<>(chants) dawned in his mind. Though the enmity bet-
<>ween Vasis2t2ha and Vis4va1mitra is seen in R2gveda, such
<>elaborate stories as seen in the Pura1n2as do not occur in
<>R2gveda. But Vis4va1mitra procured a prominent place in
<>R2gveda because this hermit rescued Suda1sa from danger
<>and forded him across rivers, and took S4unas4s4epha as
<>his son. Of these two incidents the first is not given
<>much importance in the Pura1n2as. Though the second
<>one occurs in the Pura1n2as, the version is different from [Page876-b+ 64]
<>that of R2gveda. From this it is presumed that the stories
<>taken from R2gveda underwent a thorough change before
<>they appeared in the Pura1n2as.

<HI>VIVA1HA (MARRIAGE).
<NI>1) {%General information.%} In ancient India marriage was
<>considered to be a sacrifice performed in accordance with
<>social customs. Marriage was allowed to those who had
<>completed education at the age of sixteen. (Sama1var-
<>tana). Father or teacher teaches the pupil the Vedas
<>and Veda1n3gas. When the education is completed the
<>teacher or father makes him sit on a seat decorated
<>with flowers, sandalwood etc. and do Goda1navrata. Then
<>he is offered Pan5ca1mr2ta (milk, curd, butter, honey and
<>water). This is called Sama1vartana. With this his
<>brahmacarya ends, and he is allowed to marry and
<>lead the life of a house-holder.
<NI>Marriage is a ceremony with four secondary rites Viz,
<>Kanya1da1na, S4aci1ya1ga, Viva1ha, Caturthi1karman. If the
<>husband is dead, or lost, or has renounced the world,
<>or has become a eunuch or is expelled from society, the
<>woman is allowed to take another husband. If the
<>husband dies, the wife should be given to the brother
<>of the husband. If there is no brother she could accept
<>anybody whom she likes.
<NI>2) {%Eight kinds of marriages.%} The woman and man
<>should not be of the same Gotra (family). One could
<>marry a girl who is above seven generations on the
<>paternal line and above five generations on the mater-
<>nal line. Eight types of marriages allowed in Manu-
<>smr2ti, Chapter 3, are given below:
<NI>(i) {%Bra1hma.%} A man of good qualities and good family
<>is asked to come and receive the damsel. This is
<>Bra1hma. The radiance of this marriage will give the
<>man prosperity.
<NI>(ii) {%A1rs2a.%} After getting a couple of cows from the
<>bridegroom the bride is given to him.
<NI>(iii) {%Pra1ja1patya.%} The virgin is given to the man, who
<>had requested for her hand as a duty.
<NI>(iv) {%Daiva.%} The virgin is offered to the master who is
<>engaged in performing a sacrifice.
<NI>(v) {%Ga1ndharva.%} Marriage between a man and a woman
<>with equal love on either part.
<NI>(vi) {%A1sura.%} Giving money in return for the damsel
<>and marrying her. This type is mean.
<NI>(vii) {%Ra1ks2asa.%} Carrying the damsel away by fight or
<>force.
<NI>(viii) {%Pais4a1ca.%} Marrying a damsel when she is sleeping
<>or lying unconscious.
